[**Biology**](https://xtec.gencat.cat/web/.content/curriculum/batxillerat/curriculum-171-2022/materias-de-modalitat/modalitat-ciencies-i-tecnologia/Biologia.pdf ){target="_blank"}

Advances in biology have accelerated significantly in recent decades. In this field there have been major paradigm shifts (such as the discovery of the cell, the development of the theory of evolution, the birth of molecular biology and the discovery of viruses and prions, among others) that have revolutionized the concept of a living organism and the understanding of its functioning.

The progress of the biological sciences, however, goes far beyond the mere understanding of living things. The applications of biology have led to a considerable improvement in the quality of life of humanity, by allowing, for example, the prevention and treatment of diseases that used to decimate populations, or others of new appearance, such as covid-19, for which therapies and vaccines have been developed at an unprecedented speed. In the same sense, biology also applies to and relates to genetic engineering and biotechnology and many other fields. This subject contributes to the scientific training that allows you to have a scientifically based opinion and intervene in the face of controversial facts that are part of our everyday life.

So, the subject of Biology allows you to strengthen scientific skills and thinking, contributes to strengthening the commitment to a sustainable model of development and to involve students in promoting individual and collective efforts against climate change, to achieve a model of sustainable development that contributes not only to our quality of life, but to the preservation of natural and cultural heritage, to stimulate the scientific vocation of all students, and favors the elimination of gender bias in positions of responsibility in research

The subject of Biology offers relatively advanced training, and provides students with the essential knowledge and skills for scientific work and lifelong learning and establishes the necessary foundations for starting higher studies or joining the world of work. Ultimately, this subject contributes to strengthening students' commitment and participation in democratic society.

This subject aims to provide students who take it with a sufficient foundation to understand the general principles that govern the phenomena of the natural world related to biology. For this, the subject starts from the specific skills, which aim to understand, explain and know how to mobilize knowledge, skills and attitudes, not only related to the current situation and repercussions of biology, but also to the procedures of scientific activity and their relevance in social developments, in the need for equal treatment between people and in the consistent and global nature of all scientific disciplines.

The subject must help train students to effectively manage information in the processes of selection, reworking and construction of knowledge. The approach adopted must enable students to apply the knowledge developed in an integrated way, either in the production of texts that respond to a specific format and situation or in the design of experimental research applied to the verification of a hypothesis or the development of solutions to problems applied in various contexts. In the same way, the subject must make it possible for students to adopt a suitably justified position and make coherent decisions when faced with a social, political, economic, environmental, health or scientific problem, based on the learning developed and the ability to argue, with logical and ethical criteria.

These specific skills can be summarized in: interpreting, transmitting and arguing scientific information; locate, select and compare scientific information; critically analyze the conclusions of research works; pose and solve problems related to the biological sciences; analyze the importance of healthy and sustainable habits and relate the molecular characteristics of organisms to their macroscopic characteristics.

Competences must be worked on from learning situations, in real or meaningful contexts, that invite students to reflect, collaborate and take action.

The achievement of the specific skills constitutes the basis for the student's competence assessment and will be assessed through the assessment criteria. There is no univocal and direct link between assessment criteria and knowledge. The specific skills will be assessed by putting different knowledge into action, in different situations, and the necessary flexibility will be provided to establish connections with each other. In a competence approach, the evaluation criteria and knowledge are organized around specific competences.

In the first year, it is worth highlighting the first block, *scientific project*, which deals with the basic aspects of general scientific activity: the use of scientific methodologies for the study of natural phenomena, experimentation -including the necessary instruments and their rules of use-, and the appropriate use of scientific languages ​​and relevant mathematical tools. This blog seeks to develop practical skills useful for the rest of the blogs. The second block, *history of life*, is dedicated to the study of the evolution of living beings from their origin. The third block, *biochemistry, animal and plant physiology**,* studies some of the organic and inorganic molecules characteristic of living beings. Students are introduced to the mechanisms through which animals and plants perform their vital functions; the physiology of the devices involved in the functions of nutrition and reproduction and the functioning of sensory receptors, coordination systems and effector organs in animals is analyzed and the adaptations of plants to the environmental conditions in which they develop, emphasizing the biological importance of photosynthesis. In the fourth block, *cell biology**,* cellular organization is presented, the basic processes that take place in the cell, the types of cells and their components. The fifth block, *ecology and sustainability*, is the last block and deals with the components of ecosystems, how they work and the importance of a sustainable development model.

In the second year, the knowledge is organized into six blocks. The first block, *biomolecules and metabolism*, delves into the study of organic and inorganic molecules and deals with the main metabolic routes of living beings. The second block, *molecular genetics and cell cycle*, deals with the mechanism of DNA replication and the process of gene expression, relating them to the process of cell differentiation and the stages of the cell cycle, mitosis and meiosis and their biological function. The third block, *microorganisms and acellular forms*, focuses on some of the most relevant microbial species, their metabolic diversity and ecological importance, and the study of the characteristics and infection mechanisms of acellular organic forms (viruses, viroids and prions). The fourth block, *immunology*, deals with the concept of immunity, its mechanisms and types (innate and acquired), the phases of infectious diseases and the study of pathologies of the immune system. In the fifth block, *biotechnology*, methods of manipulating living beings or their components are studied for technological application in different fields, such as medicine, agriculture or ecology, among others. Finally, the sixth block, *evolution*, addresses the study of the biological mechanisms through which evolution works.

The knowledge that is described must be worked on from a competence approach, so that it constitutes a means for the development of key competences and not simply an end in itself.

It should be noted that Biology is a subject of a scientific nature and, as such, it is recommended to teach it by linking it to the students' reality, in a practical and meaningful way and following an interdisciplinary approach. For this reason, the proposed methodology is the use of learning situations that connect with real contexts. As a conclusion, it should be noted that the ultimate purpose of Biology is to contribute to a greater degree of exercise of key skills by the students, in order to significantly expand their academic, professional, social and personal horizons.

**Specific skills**

**Competition 1**

**Interpret, communicate information and data from scientific works, and argue accurately and using different formats, to analyze concepts, processes, methods, experiments or results of the biological sciences.**

**Evaluation criteria**

| 1st year | 2nd year |
| --- | --- |
| 1.1 Critically analyze concepts and processes related to the knowledge of Biology, selecting and interpreting information in different formats (models, graphs, tables, diagrams, formulas, schemes or others). 1.2 Communicate information or reasoned opinions related to the knowledge of the subject of Biology by transmitting them in a clear and rigorous manner, using the appropriate terminology and format (models, graphs, tables, reports, diagrams, formulas, digital content or others) and responding in a well-founded manner to questions that may arise during the process. 1.3 Argue about aspects related to the knowledge of the subject of Biology, defending a position in a reasoned way and with an open, flexible, receptive attitude, respectful of the opinion of others and based on scientific knowledge. | 1.1 Critically analyze concepts and processes related to the knowledge of Biology, selecting and interpreting information in different formats (models, graphs, tables, diagrams, formulas, schemes or others). 1.2 Communicate information or reasoned opinions related to the knowledge of the subject of Biology, transmitting them in a clear and rigorous manner, using the appropriate terminology and format (models, graphics, tables, videos, reports, diagrams, formulas, schemes, symbols, digital content or others) and responding in a well-founded and precise manner to questions that may arise during the process. 1.3 Argue about aspects related to the knowledge of the subject of Biology, considering the strengths and weaknesses of different positions in a reasoned way and with an open, flexible, receptive and respectful attitude towards the opinion of others and based on scientific knowledge. |

Communication is an essential aspect of scientific progress, given that advances and discoveries are rarely the product of the work of isolated individuals, but of collaborative teams, often of an interdisciplinary nature. Knowledge creation only occurs when discoveries are published and allowed to be reviewed and expanded by the scientific community.

Communication therefore plays a prominent role, because it is essential for collaboration and the dissemination of knowledge, and contributes to considerably speeding up advances and discoveries. Scientific communication generally seeks the exchange of relevant information in a way that is as efficient and simple as possible, using different formats such as graphics, formulas, texts, reports or models, among others.

This competence refers to the development by students of the skills necessary to extract the most relevant ideas from information of a scientific nature (in the form of articles, diagrams, tables, graphs, etc.) and to communicate them in a simple, precise and reliable way, using varied formats (oral presentation, virtual platforms, presentation of slides and posters, among others), both analogically and by digital means.

Therefore, communication in the context of this subject requires the mobilization of not only linguistic skills, but also mathematical, digital and logical reasoning. Students must interpret and transmit scientific content, as well as form their own opinion about them, based on reasoning and evidence, and argue by defending their position in a well-founded way and enriching it with the points of view and evidence provided by others.

This competence also aims to enhance argumentation, which is essential for the social and professional development of students. Argumentation in debates, forums or other ways gives the opportunity to defend, in a logical and well-founded way, one's own positions, but also to understand and assimilate the ideas of other people. Argumentation is a way of collective thinking that enriches those who participate, and allows them to develop resilience in the face of challenges, as well as the flexibility to change their own ideas in the face of other people's arguments. Likewise, argumentation, carried out correctly, promotes tolerance and respect.

In conclusion, scientific communication is a complex process, in which various skills are combined in an integrated manner and knowledge is mobilized, and it requires an open and tolerant attitude towards the interlocutor. All this is necessary not only for the work in the scientific career, but also constitutes an essential aspect for the personal, social and professional development of every human being.

**Competition 2**

**Identify, select, organize and critically evaluate information, contrasting its reliability to solve questions posed autonomously and create content related to the biological sciences.**

**Evaluation criteria**

| 1st year | 2nd year |
| --- | --- |
| 2.1 Raise and resolve issues related to subject knowledge, locating and citing appropriate sources and selecting, organizing and critically analyzing information. 2.2 Contrast and justify the credibility of information related to the knowledge of the subject, using reliable sources and adopting a critical and skeptical attitude towards interested information, without proven authorship or without a scientific basis, such as pseudoscience, conspiracy theories, unfounded beliefs, rumors, etc. 2.3 Argue about the contribution of science to society and the work of the people who dedicate themselves to it, reflecting on gender bias in the sciences and understanding research as a collective and interdisciplinary task in constant evolution influenced by the political context and economic resources. | 2.1 Raise and solve questions and create content related to the knowledge of the subject of Biology by locating and citing appropriate sources and selecting, organizing and critically analyzing the information. 2.2 Contrast and justify the credibility of information related to the knowledge of the subject, using reliable sources, providing data and adopting a critical and skeptical attitude towards interested information, without proven authorship or without a scientific basis, such as pseudoscience, conspiracy theories, unfounded beliefs, rumors, etc. |

Obtaining relevant information to resolve doubts, acquire new knowledge or check the reliability of statements or news is an essential skill for citizens of the 21st century.

All scientific research begins with a compilation of publications in the field to be studied. That is why it is necessary to know and use reliable sources and to search for them, and to select the relevant information to answer the questions raised.

Most of the reliable sources of information are accessible through the Internet, so the use of different digital search and communication platforms will be promoted through this competition. However, truthful information coexists with rumours, conspiracy theories and incomplete or pseudo-scientific information. For this reason, it is vitally important that students develop a critical spirit and contrast and evaluate the information obtained.

In addition, lifelong learning requires a critical sense to select the right sources or institutions, to sift through the information and keep what is relevant according to the intended purpose. The skill to make this selection is, therefore, of great importance not only for the exercise of scientific professions, but also for the development of any type of professional career, for active democratic participation and even for the social and emotional well-being of people.

**Competition 3**

**Design and develop research projects related to biology and critically analyze the results of these projects and of research and dissemination work, checking if they follow the steps of scientific methodology, to assess the reliability of the conclusions.**

**Evaluation criteria**

| 1st year | 2nd year |
| --- | --- |
| 3.1 Ask questions and formulate hypotheses that can be answered or contrasted using scientific methods and try to explain biological phenomena, and make predictions about these phenomena. 3.2 Assess the reliability of the conclusions of an own research work in accordance with the interpretation of the results obtained. 3.3 Design experimentation, data collection and analysis of biological phenomena, and select the necessary instruments, in such a way that they allow answering specific researchable questions and contrasting a proposed hypothesis minimizing biases as much as possible. 3.4 Carry out experiments and take quantitative and qualitative data on biological phenomena, selecting and using the appropriate instruments, tools or techniques with correctness and precision. 3.5 Interpret and analyze results obtained in the research project using, when necessary, mathematical and technological tools and recognizing their scope and limitations to obtain reasoned and grounded conclusions or assess the impossibility of doing so. 3.6 Establish collaborations inside and outside the educational center in the different phases of the scientific project to work more efficiently, using the appropriate technological tools, valuing the importance of cooperation in research, respecting diversity and promoting inclusion. | 3.1 Assess the reliability of the conclusions of a research or scientific dissemination work related to the knowledge of the subject in accordance with the interpretation of the results obtained. 3.2 Argue, using concrete examples, about the contribution of science to society and the work of the people who have dedicated themselves to it, reflecting on gender bias in the sciences and understanding research as a collective and interdisciplinary task in constant evolution influenced by the political context and economic resources. |

Scientific knowledge is built from evidence obtained from objective observation and experimentation and its purpose is to explain the functioning of the world around us and to provide solutions to the problems of our time. Scientific methods are based on formulating questions about the natural or social environment, designing and implementing appropriate strategies to answer them, interpreting and analyzing results, drawing conclusions, and communicating.

Critical thinking is probably one of the most important skills for human development and the basis of the spirit of overcoming and improvement. In the scientific field, it is essential, among others, for the review of research works, which is the pillar on which the rigor and reliability of science is based. Although critical thinking must begin to be worked on from the earliest educational stages, it reaches a significant degree of development in high school, and progress in this specific competence contributes to its improvement. In addition, the analysis of the conclusions of a scientific work in relation to the observable results involves mobilizing in students, not only critical thinking, but also communicative and digital skills and logical reasoning.

Setting up situations in which students have the opportunity to apply the steps of the different methods used in science contributes to developing their curiosity, critical sense, entrepreneurial spirit and skills for collaborative work. In addition, it allows you to understand in depth the difference between an impression or opinion and evidence, to deal with different information with an open mind and insight and to accept uncertainty and respond appropriately.

Likewise, the analytical attitude and the cultivation of reasonable doubt, which are developed through this specific competence, are useful in non-scientific contexts and prepare students for the recognition of fallacies, rumors and pseudoscientific information and to form their own opinion based on reasoning and evidence, thus contributing positively to their personal and professional integration and their participation in democratic society.

**Competition 4**

**Apply the learnings in an integrated way and the various forms of reasoning specific to science, to pose and solve problems related to the biological sciences, searching for and using the appropriate strategies, critically analyzing the solutions and reformulating the procedure, if necessary.**

**Evaluation criteria**

| 1st year | 2nd year |
| --- | --- |
| 4.1 Solve problems or explain biological processes using varied resources such as knowledge, data and information, logical reasoning, computational thinking or digital resources. 4.2 Critically analyze the solution to problems on biological phenomena, and modify the procedures used or conclusions obtained if this solution is not viable or in the face of new data provided or found later. | 4.1 Explain phenomena related to the knowledge of the subject by posing and solving problems, searching for and using the appropriate strategies and resources. 4.2 Critically analyze the solution to a problem using the knowledge of the subject of Biology and reformulate the procedures used or the conclusions if this solution was not viable or in the face of new data provided or found later. |

Problem solving is an inherent part of basic and applied science. Empirical sciences are built by contrasting reasoning (hypotheses) through experimentation or observation. Scientific progress is limited, therefore, by the dexterity in the intellectual exercise of creating hypotheses and the technical and human capacity to test them experimentally. Moreover, the path to discoveries and breakthroughs is rarely straight and is often hampered by unexpected situations and problems of a different nature. That is why it is essential that, when faced with difficulties, people dedicated to science show creativity, skills for the search for new strategies or the use of varied tools, openness to collaboration and resilience to continue despite the lack of immediate success.

This specific competence refers to the integrated application of learning and the use of reasoning as a basis for problem solving. However, it should be noted that, as a novelty with regard to the previous stage, it is intended that students look for new resolution strategies when the strategies they have acquired are not sufficient. For this reason, it will be necessary to use different technological tools and resources, a positive attitude towards challenges and situations of uncertainty and resilience to continue trying new ways of resolution in case of initial lack of success, or with the intention of improving the results.

That is why it is important to work on the initiative in students so that they raise new questions or problems that can be solved using reasoning and other strategies.

Problem solving is an essential skill in a scientific career, given that people engaged in science often face great challenges and setbacks that make the path to their goals tortuous.

Likewise, this specific competence is necessary in many other contexts of professional and personal life as it contributes to the intellectual and emotional maturity of students and, ultimately, to the formation of fully integrated citizens committed to the improvement of society.

**Competition 5**

**Design, promote and execute environmental conservation initiatives based on scientific foundations and analyze the impacts of human activities on the environment or the availability of resources, based on field observations and information in different formats to promote and adopt habits compatible with sustainable development.**

**Evaluation criteria**

| 1st year | 2nd year |
| --- | --- |
| 5.1 Analyze the ecological, social and economic causes and consequences of the main environmental problems from an individual, local and global perspective, conceiving them as great challenges for humanity and based on scientific data and the knowledge of the subject of Biology. 5.2 Propose and justify the need to adopt habits and carry out sustainable and healthy initiatives at the local level and argue about the positive effects and the urgency of adopting them based on the knowledge of the subject. | 5.1 Argue about the importance of adopting healthy habits and a sustainable development model, based on the principles of biology, particularly molecular biology, and relate them to macroscopic processes. |

Currently, environmental degradation leads to the destruction of natural resources at a much higher rate than regeneration. To slow the progress of these negative trends and avoid their catastrophic consequences, individual and collective actions by citizens, states and corporations are needed. For this reason, it is essential to know the ecological, scientific, social and economic value of the natural world and to understand that environmental degradation is synonymous with inequality, climate refugees, natural disasters and other types of humanitarian crises.

For these reasons, it is essential that students develop this specific competence and thus know the foundations that justify the urgent need to implement a sustainable development model and lead innovative initiatives and projects to promote and adopt sustainable habits in the individual and collective sphere. Developing this specific competence also allows students to deepen the study of human physiology and thus propose and adopt habits that contribute to maintaining and improving health and quality of life. This aspect is particularly important given the upward trend in sedentary habits and the consumption of hypercaloric foods, which has serious consequences for the health of citizens of the developed world.

Throughout high school, students will be able to focus on these issues progressively in greater depth. The study of the importance of ecosystems and certain organisms will be approached from the knowledge of the biochemical reactions they carry out and their relevance on a planetary scale. In this way, the molecular world will be connected with the macroscopic world. This specific competence also seeks for students to take initiatives aimed at analyzing their own habits and those of members of the educational community, develop a critical attitude towards these habits based on the foundations of molecular biology and propose measures for positive change towards a healthier and more sustainable way of life.

The importance of this specific competence lies in the importance of adopting a sustainable development model, which constitutes one of the biggest and most important challenges facing humanity today. To be able to realize this ambitious goal, it is necessary for society to achieve a deep understanding of the functioning of biological systems in order to be able to appreciate their value. In this way, habits will be adopted and responsible attitudes will be taken aimed at the conservation of ecosystems and biodiversity and the saving of resources, which at the same time will improve human health and physical and mental well-being in the individual and collective sphere.

**Competition 6**

**Describe, integrate and relate the main characteristic processes of living beings to justify the complexity of life and distinguish it from what is inert.**

**Evaluation criteria**

| 1st year | 2nd year |
| --- | --- |
| 6.1 Identify and differentiate the different biomolecules of living beings. 6.2 Experimentally identify different types of biomolecules and relate them to biological structures and foods. 6.3 Justify the concept of cell as a structural and functional unit of living beings. | 6.1 Explain the characteristics and vital processes of living beings by analyzing their biomolecules, their functions, the biochemical interactions between biomolecules and their metabolic reactions. 6.2 Apply analytical methodologies in the laboratory using the appropriate materials with precision. 6.3 Justify the importance of the processing of matter and energy for the maintenance of life at different levels (cellular, organism, ecosystem) and for its capacity for self-preservation. 6.4 Argue the importance of the genetic program for the life of living beings and its relationship with biological evolution. |

In the 19th century, the first synthesis of an organic molecule in the laboratory made it possible to connect biology and chemistry and marked a change in the scientific paradigm that was later reinforced with the description of DNA as a molecule that carries genetic information.

Living beings depend on the processing of the matter and energy they incorporate from their environment. This processing is carried out thanks to the existence of a genetic program that gives them the ability to maintain themselves, with self-preserving activities, as a response to external conditions. In addition, the transformation of this genetic program is one of the bases of biological evolution.

The voluntary choice of the Biology subject at this stage is probably linked to scientific concerns and the intention to do tertiary studies in the biomedical or environmental field. For these reasons, this specific competence is essential for high school students and allows them to connect the molecular world with the macroscopic one, understand the complexity of the existence of life, acquire a complete global vision of living organisms and develop the necessary skills to formulate hypotheses and solve problems related to the different disciplines that derive from biology.

**know**

Knowledge, understood as the set of knowledge, skills, values ​​and attitudes, is formulated in relation to contexts in which competence learning can be developed. Teachers can incorporate alternative contexts if they consider it relevant. In order to facilitate learning and the development of the corresponding specific skills, teachers can assess the possibility of organizing the knowledge of the subject, or of the different subjects coordinated in an area, based on situations.

The situations make it possible to program the course of any level, subject or field from a collection or sequence of challenges, contexts and circumstances of the real world, from which derive questions that need to be answered and that intertwine knowledge, that is, knowledge, skills, values and attitudes, with the capacities that support the competence approach to learning, which modifies the usual planning of the acquisition of knowledge and competences based on academic logic specific to the areas of knowledge or subjects, embodied in the traditional sequence of disciplinary subjects. It aims to approach the learner's logic to give meaning to their learning based on the sequence of relevant contexts embodied in the situations.

**First year**

**Scientific Project**

- Approach with a scientific perspective of researchable hypotheses, questions, problems and conjectures in the school context.
- Strategies for the search for information, collaboration, communication and interaction with scientific institutions: digital tools, presentation formats of processes, results and ideas (slides, graphics, videos, posters, reports and others), in the resolution of researchable problems.
- Reliable sources of information: search, recognition and use in experimental research or observational studies formulated in the classroom.
- Laboratory or field scientific experiences in the school context: design, planning and implementation. Hypothesis contrast. Experimental controls.
- Results analysis methods: organization, representation and statistical tools, applicable to the proposed research.
- Scientific communication strategies: scientific vocabulary, formats (reports, videos, models, graphics and others) and digital tools.
- The scientific work and people dedicated to science: contribution to the biological, geological and environmental sciences and social importance. The role of women in science. Historical cases with gender bias.
- The historical evolution of scientific knowledge: science as a collective, interdisciplinary task and in continuous construction.

**Life Story**

- Contrast of different hypotheses about the origin of living beings.
- Analysis of the changes in the large groups of living beings throughout the history of the Earth in view of evolutionary theories.
- Comparison of the main taxonomic groups according to their fundamental characteristics, with an evolutionary approach.

**Biochemistry, animal and plant physiology**

- Differentiation between organic and inorganic biomolecules and their general characteristics.
- Water and mineral salts: relationship between their chemical characteristics and biological functions.
- Analysis of the chemical characteristics, isomers, bonds and functions of monosaccharides (pentoses, hexoses in their linear and cyclic forms), disaccharides and polysaccharides with greater biological relevance.
- Differentiation between lipids with and without fatty acids: chemical characteristics, types and biological functions of the different types of lipids.
- The function of nutrition in animals: biological importance and structures involved in different taxonomic groups, with an evolutionary approach.
- Recognition of the importance of vitamins and salts as enzyme cofactors and the need to incorporate them into the human diet.
- Laboratory identification and study of the different nutrients in the human diet. Analysis of the reliability of food labels.
- The function of nutrition in plants: photosynthesis, its general balance and importance for life on Earth. Comparison of the composition, formation and transport mechanisms of raw and processed sap.
- The relationship function in animals: physiology and functioning of coordination systems (nervous and endocrine), sensory receptors and effector organs, with an evolutionary approach.
- The relationship function in plants: types of plant responses to stimuli and the influence of phytohormones (auxins, cytokinins, ethylene, etc.).
- The function of reproduction in animals: biological importance, types, structures involved in different taxonomic groups, with an evolutionary approach.
- The function of reproduction: sexual and asexual reproduction, evolutionary relevance, biological cycles, types of asexual reproduction, processes involved in sexual reproduction (pollination, fertilization, seed and fruit dispersal) and the relationship with the ecosystem.

**Cell Biology**

- Analysis of cell theory and its biological implications.
- Differentiation of images obtained by optical and electron microscopy, taking into account the resolution power of each and the sample preparation techniques.
- Analysis of the ultrastructure of the plasma membrane and relation to its properties.
- Analysis of the osmotic process and impact on animal, plant and prokaryotic cells.
- Basic functional analysis of the organelles of the eukaryotic cell (animal and plant).
- Analysis of the different transport mechanisms through the plasma membrane (simple and facilitated diffusion, active transport, endocytosis and exocytosis), relating each to the properties of the transported molecules.
- Energy capture and utilization strategies.

**Ecology and sustainability**

- The environment as an economic and social engine: importance and need for the adoption of a sustainable development model, based on cases from the local and global environment.
- The sustainability of everyday activities: use of sustainability indicators, compatible and consistent lifestyles with a sustainable development model. Ecological footprint concept.
- The shift towards a sustainable development model: local and global initiatives.
- The dynamics of ecosystems: energy flows, matter cycles (carbon, nitrogen, phosphorus and sulphur) and trophic relationships. Solving problems raised at the local and global level.
- Climate change: its relationship with the carbon cycle, causes and consequences on health, economy, ecology and society.

**Second year**

**Biomolecules and metabolism**

- Identification of biomolecules based on their chemical structure and its relationship with the functions they perform.
- Classification of biomolecules according to the functions they perform.
- Metabolism concept. Comparison between anabolism and catabolism.
- Relationship between the chemical characteristics, structure and biological function of proteins, analyzing the importance of their biocatalytic role.
- Overview of the different processes involved in anaerobic cellular respiration
- (glycolysis and fermentation) and aerobic (β-oxidation of fatty acids, Krebs cycle, electron transport chain and oxidative phosphorylation).
- Analysis of the biological significance, on a molecular and cellular scale, of the main catabolic routes. Metabolism as a way of processing matter and energy.
- Comparison between aerobic and anaerobic metabolism: comparative calculation of energy yield and reflection on the efficiency of each.
- Analysis of the main routes of heterotrophic (amino acid, protein and fatty acid synthesis) and autotrophic (photosynthesis and chemosynthesis) anabolism and their biological importance.
- Analysis of fermentations as partial degradation of biomolecules and their application in food production.

**Genetics and cell cycle**

- Relationship between the chemical characteristics, structure and biological function of the different types of nucleic acids.
- Analysis of the DNA replication mechanism using the prokaryotic model.
- Analysis, using a prokaryotic model, of the general stages of gene expression and the characteristics of the genetic code and solving related problems.
- Solving problems of monohybridism and dihybridism in cases of autosomal and sex-linked inheritance.
- Interpretation of evolution as a change in gene frequency, while solving simple quantitative genetics problems.
- Argument on the relationship between mutations, DNA replication, evolution and biodiversity.
- Assessment of the importance of the regulation of gene expression in cell differentiation.
- Comparison of the general characteristics of the genome and gene expression in prokaryotes and eukaryotes.
- Sequencing the phases of the cell cycle and analysis of the regulatory mechanisms.
- Comparison of meiosis and mitosis: phases and function.
- Study of cancer and the relationship with mutations and alteration of the cell cycle.

**Microorganisms and acellular forms**

- Differentiation between bacteria and archaebacteria.
- Comparison of some of the forms of bacterial metabolism and the ecological importance it has in symbioses and biogeochemical cycles.
- Analysis of microorganisms as causal agents of infectious diseases and reflection on zoonoses and epidemics.
- Recognition of the presence of bacteria in the microbiota, everyday life and their applications. Use of microorganisms in industrial processes: agriculture, pharmacy, food and bioremediation.
- Sterilization and isolation techniques and cultivation of microorganisms.
- Analysis of the mechanisms of horizontal genetic transfer in bacteria and the problem of antibiotic resistance.
- Comparison of the characteristics and infection mechanisms of the different acellular forms (viruses, viroids and prions) and their biological importance.

**Immunology**

- Concept of immunity. Application to current and relevant historical cases.
- Identification of the different types of external barriers that hinder the entry of pathogens. Examples related to everyday life.
- Differentiation between innate and specific immunity, based on relevant examples.
- Comparison between the mechanisms of action of humoral and cellular immunity. Application to cases close to students.
- Comparison of the working mechanisms of artificial and natural, passive and active immunity. Effects of vaccination on individuals and populations in relevant current and historical cases.
- Analysis of the phases of infectious diseases, based on recent or current cases.
- Main pathologies of the immune system: causes and clinical relevance.

**Biotechnology**

- Analysis of the most relevant genetic engineering techniques (PCR, restriction enzymes, molecular cloning, CRISPR-CAS9 and others) and their applications.
- Argument on the importance of biotechnology and its applications in different areas (health, agriculture, environment, new materials, food industry, etc.) highlighting the role of microorganisms.

**Evolution**

- Justification of evolution as a fact.
- Review of historical background: Lamarckism and Darwinism. Identification and analysis of the sources of genetic variability: mutations and genetic recombination.
- Current perspectives on evolutionary mechanisms.

<h2 class="accordion-header" id="headingFis">

[**Physics**](https://xtec.gencat.cat/web/.content/curriculum/batxillerat/curriculum-171-2022/materias-de-modalitat/modalitat-ciencies-i-tecnologia/Fisica.pdf){target="_blank"}


The teaching of Physics at high school completes the scientific training that students have acquired throughout compulsory secondary education and actively contributes to students acquiring a rich and quality scientific cultural base that allows them to develop with confidence and judgment in a society that demands scientific and technical profiles for research and the world of work, while giving them tools to analyze the reality that surrounds them.

Physics, as a discipline that studies nature, is responsible for understanding and describing the universe, from the phenomena that occur in the microcosm to those that occur in the macrocosm. Matter, energy and interactions behave differently in different scenarios, and this means that the models, principles and laws that students must apply to explain nature must be adjusted to the scale of work and that the answers or explanations they find are approximate and conditioned by the context, but that is no less rigorous. This should also help to demystify that physics is complex, showing that many of the phenomena that occur in everyday life can be understood and explained through accessible physical models and laws.

Achieving that the study of these phenomena is rewarding contributes to forming critical citizens with an adequate scientific basis. Physics is present in the technological advances that facilitate better economic development of society, which currently prioritizes sustainability and seeks solutions to serious environmental problems. Continuous innovation drives this technological development and the students, who will partly make up this scientific community, must have the skills to contribute to it and the knowledge, skills and attitudes that shape them.

Encouraging students' curiosity about the workings and knowledge of nature is the starting point for achieving successes that will have a positive impact on social development based on criteria of equality, social justice and sustainability.

The integrative approach in the scientific, technological and mathematical field that is intended to be given to the subject of Physics throughout secondary education and at high school prepares students to face a future that is oriented towards achieving the goals of sustainable development and the challenges of the 21st century in a critical way.

Many students will probably pursue professions that they cannot even imagine yet, and that is why the curriculum of this subject is open and competitive, and its purpose is not only to contribute to deepening the acquisition of knowledge, skills and attitudes in science, but also to help students to design a personal and professional profile that allows them to fully develop in a complex and changing society, where information management and the ability to issue reasoned and critical judgments will be elements fundamental

The curricular design of the subject is based on specific skills, the development of which gives students the ability to develop knowledge, skills and advanced scientific attitudes. In this sense, the experimental nature of physics must be kept in mind, and for this reason the use of experimental methodologies and tools is proposed, such as the mathematical formulation of laws and principles, the appropriate and skillful use of measuring and data collection instruments, whether analog or digital, as well as all the other resources that can facilitate the understanding of the concepts and phenomena of physics: virtual laboratories, simulations, mobile applications, historical texts, dissemination articles, etc.

This subject must help train students to effectively manage information in the processes of selection, reworking and construction of knowledge. The approach adopted must enable students to apply the knowledge developed in an integrated way, either in the production of texts that respond to a specific format and situation or the design of an experimental research applied to the verification of a hypothesis or the development of solutions to problems applied in various contexts. In the same way, the subject must make it possible for students, based on the learning developed and the ability to argue, with logical and ethical criteria, to adopt a suitably justified position and make coherent decisions when faced with a social, political, economic, environmental, health, scientific, etc. problem.

Finally, the competencies also aim to encourage teamwork, similar to the normal functioning of the scientific community, to achieve committed people who use science for lifelong learning, environmental development, community good and progress towards an egalitarian, healthy and sustainable society.

Competences must be worked on from learning situations, in real or meaningful contexts, that invite students to reflect, collaborate and take action.

The achievement of the specific skills constitutes the basis for the student's competence assessment and will be assessed through the assessment criteria. There is no univocal and direct link between assessment criteria and knowledge. Specific skills will be assessed by putting different knowledge into action, in different situations, providing the necessary flexibility to establish connections with each other. In a competence approach, the evaluation criteria and knowledge are organized around specific competences.

Accompanying the specific skills of this subject are the assessment criteria, directly linked to the specific skills, which explain the assessment of the skills and knowledge that need to be developed, measure the degree of development of these skills and specify the learning we want to identify in the students and the way to do it. Their character is markedly competitive and makes them evaluators not only of theoretical content, but also of the skills and attitudes that students must acquire in order to develop in a society that demands a critical spirit both in the face of scientific questions and others of a social nature, in which science plays an important role. The teaching staff must contextualize and make these criteria more flexible in accordance with the circumstances of their activity.

The development of specific skills is based on key skills and subject knowledge, which are structured in blocks that include essential knowledge, skills and attitudes. For this reason, it is chosen to formulate the knowledge linked to a capacity and in a context in which they must be developed. The teaching staff can develop an alternative context, if they consider it appropriate.

The different blocks of knowledge in the high school Physics subject are focused on completing and relating the teachings of previous stages, so that students can acquire a global perception of the different lines of work in physics and their various applications.

In the first year, the *kinematics* block includes an in-depth study of the kinematics block with a vector approach, so that the mathematical load of this unit gradually adapts to the requirements of the students' maturative development. In addition, the study of a greater number of movements allows him to expand the perspectives of this branch of mechanics.

It is just as important to know the causes of movement, which is why the following blog, *statics and dynamics*, presents the knowledge and skills corresponding to statics and dynamics. Taking advantage of the vector study of the previous block, students apply this tool to describe the effects of forces on particles and on rigid solids in terms of studying the moment that produces a force, deducing what the causes are in each case.

The *energy* blog presents the knowledge as a continuation of what was studied in the previous stage, and goes deeper into work, power and mechanical energy and conservation. It also introduces the basic aspects of thermodynamics that allow them to understand the operation of simple thermodynamic systems and their most immediate applications. All this aimed at understanding the importance of the concept of energy in our daily lives, and in relation to other scientific and technological disciplines.

In the second year, the following two blocks, *gravitational field* and *electromagnetic field*, refer to classical field theory, with the study of the gravitational field and electromagnetism. In the first case, they will study, using the appropriate mathematical tools to give the block sufficient rigor, the interactions that are generated between particles with mass and their relationship with some of the knowledge from previous courses about their mechanics, their energy and the principles of conservation. Then, learning about electromagnetism is incorporated, based on the description of electric and magnetic fields, both static and time-varying, and their characteristics and technological, biosanitary and industrial applications.

The following blog, *vibrations and waves*, presents knowledge related to vibrations and waves, considering oscillatory motion as a generator of disturbances and their propagation in space-time through a wave motion. The study is completed with the detailed analysis of the conservation of energy in waves and its application in the field of concrete examples, such as sound waves and electromagnetic waves, and thus introduces the study of the processes specific to physical optics and geometric optics.

With the last block, *relativistic, quantum, nuclear and particle physics*, the general panorama of the physics of the present and the future is shown. The knowledge, skills and attitudes of quantum physics and particle physics are exposed. Under the fundamental principles of relativistic physics, this blog explains the constitution of matter and the description of the processes that take place when studying science on a microscopic scale. This blog will allow students to approach the frontiers of physics and will open their curiosity – the best engine for their learning – seeing that there are still many questions to be solved and many challenges that must be addressed from the research and development of this science.

This High School Physics curriculum is presented as an integrative proposal, which reinforces the foundations of learning the procedures and methodologies specific to science, while highlighting the students' learning skills and encouraging their interest and curiosity towards the development of scientific knowledge and the analysis of its impact on society.

The incorporation of contextualized proposals, in line with the integrative approach, aims to promote more meaningful and realistic learning, which should enable students to generate curiosity for science research and be trained to meet the social, technological and industrial demands that the present and the near future offer us, while becoming an active part of a citizenry with critical and socially responsible capacity.

**Specific skills**

**Competition 1**

**Analyze phenomena and solve problems based on close situations by using the theories, principles and laws of physics, paying attention to their experimental basis, theoretical description and mathematical development, to demonstrate their involvement in the development of technology, the economy, society and environmental sustainability.**

**Evaluation criteria**

| 1st year | 2nd year |
| --- | --- |
| 1.1 Apply the theories, principles and laws of physics in the analysis of everyday phenomena, understanding the causes that produce them and explaining them using a variety of supports and means of communication.  1.2 Solve problems posed from everyday situations, applying laws and scientific theories to find and argue the solutions and expressing the results appropriately.  1.3 Identify problematic situations in the everyday environment, take initiatives and look for sustainable solutions from physics, critically analyzing the impact produced on society and the environment. | 1.1 Recognize the relevance and contributions of physics in the development of science, technology, the economy, society and environmental sustainability, using appropriately the scientific foundations related to these areas.  1.2 Solve problems posed from everyday situations experimentally and analytically, using principles, laws and theories of physics. |

Using the principles, laws and theories of physics requires a broad knowledge of their theoretical foundations. The ability to understand and describe, through experimentation or the use of mathematical developments, the interactions that occur between bodies and systems in nature, allows, at the same time, to develop scientific thinking to build new knowledge applied to solving problems in the different contexts in which physics intervenes. This implies appreciating physics as a field of knowledge with important implications in technology, the economy, society and environmental sustainability.

In this way, based on the understanding of the implications of physics in other fields of everyday life, the ability to form a grounded opinion on the situations that affect each context is acquired, which is necessary to develop critical thinking and an attitude of contributing to progress through the acquired scientific knowledge, providing sustainable solutions.

**Competition 2**

**Analyze the immediate environment and predict its evolution based on the models, theories and laws of physics by formulating researchable questions, investigating and searching for evidence to propose general solutions to everyday problems related to the practical applications of physics in the technological, industrial and biosanitary fields.**

**Evaluation criteria**

| 1st year | 2nd year |
| --- | --- |
| 2.1 Formulate and verify hypotheses as responses to different problems and observations of the immediate environment, through the skillful use of experimental work, inquiry, the search for evidence and logical-mathematical reasoning.  2.2 Use different methods to find the answer to a single question or observation, comparing the results obtained to ensure consistency and reliability.  2.3 Integrate the models, theories and laws of physics in the process of validating the formulated hypotheses, applying qualitative and quantitative relationships between the different variables, so that the process is more reliable and consistent with scientific knowledge. | 2.1 Analyze and understand the evolution of natural systems, using models, laws and theories of physics.  2.2 Infer general solutions to general problems based on the analysis of particular situations and the variables on which they depend.  2.3 Use the models, laws and theories of physics to analyze and understand the general operation of practical applications and products useful to society in the technological, industrial and biosanitary fields. |

The study of physics, as a natural science, must provide the ability to analyze phenomena that occur in the closest natural environment. For this reason, it is necessary to adopt the models, theories and laws that form the fundamental pillars of this field of knowledge, and which at the same time make it possible to predict the evolution of systems and natural objects. At the same time, this adoption occurs when the ability to relate observed phenomena in everyday situations to the foundations and principles of physics is developed.

Thus, based on the analysis of various particular situations, the ability to infer general solutions to everyday problems is acquired, which can result in practical applications necessary for society and which will give rise to products and benefits through their development from the technological, industrial or biosanitary field.

**Competition 3**

**Use with propriety, correctness and fluency, in the different communication registers of science, the language of physics with the mathematical formulation of its principles, magnitudes, units of measurement, etc., to demonstrate the need to establish a communication tool between scientific communities and in research.**

**Evaluation criteria**

| 1st year | 2nd year |
| --- | --- |
| 3.1 Use and relate rigorously the International System of Units (SI) and other systems of units, correctly using their notation and their equivalences, recognizing their role as an effective communication tool among the scientific community.  3.2 Extract, interpret and express information from different formats relating to a specific process, relating the information to each other and extracting the most relevant information during the resolution of a problem.  3.3 Put into practice the knowledge acquired in scientific experimentation in the laboratory or other environments, including the correct use of measuring and data collection devices and the basic regulations for use, as well as the safety rules specific to these spaces. | 3.1 Apply scientific principles, laws and theories in the critical analysis of physical processes in the environment, such as those observed and those published in different media, analyzing, understanding and explaining in a reasoned way the causes that produce them.  3.2 Rigorously use the units of physical variables expressed in the International System of Units (SI) and other relevant unit systems, correctly using their notation and equivalences, as well as the preparation and appropriate interpretation of graphs that relate physical variables, recognizing their role as an effective communication tool among the scientific community.  3.3 Express the results in an appropriate way, arguing the solutions obtained, in the resolution of exercises and problems defined from situations based on realistic or ideal contexts. |

The development of this specific competence aims to transfer to the students a set of criteria for the use of formalisms with a scientific basis, with the aim of being able to properly propose and discuss the resolution of physics problems and their applications in the world around them. In addition, it is intended that they value the universality of mathematical language and its formulation as a tool to exchange physical approaches and their resolutions in different communication environments.

Introducing students to collaborative participation among the scientific community requires a specific, rigorous and common code that ensures the clarity of the messages exchanged between members.

**Competition 4**

**Select and critically evaluate information and resources, in different formats and platforms, both in individual and collective work, to create scientific and dissemination content related to physics and argue about its role in society.**

**Evaluation criteria**

| 1st year | 2nd year |
| --- | --- |
| 4.1 Interact with other members of the educational community through different learning environments, real and virtual, using autonomously and efficiently various resources, traditional analogue and digital, in a rigorous and respectful manner and critically analyzing all contributions 4.2 Manage autonomously and versatilely, individually and in groups, information and the creation of content, with a scientific basis, using with judgment and rigor the most appropriate sources and tools, thus improving learning own and collective. | 4.1 Consult, prepare and exchange scientific and informative materials in different formats with other members of the learning environment, using digital platforms autonomously and efficiently.  4.2 Use digital and traditional media in a critical, ethical and responsible way as a way to enrich learning and individual and collective work and to recognize the presence of physics in society. |

Among the skills that need to be acquired in today's new teaching-learning contexts is the use of virtual learning platforms and environments. These platforms serve as a repository of resources and materials of different types and in different formats, and are useful for learning physics, as well as means for individual and social learning. It is therefore necessary to develop the ability to use these resources autonomously and efficiently to facilitate self-regulated learning and at the same time be responsible in interactions with other students and with the teaching staff.

At the same time, the production and exchange of scientific and informative materials allow physics to be brought closer to society in a creative way, presenting it as an accessible field of knowledge.

**Competition 5**

**Apply work and inquiry techniques specific to physics such as experimentation in real or virtual environments, logical-mathematical reasoning, individually or in collaborative environments similar to those of the scientific community, to recognize the role of physics and predict the influence of its advances in a society based on ethical and sustainable values.**

**Evaluation criteria**

| 1st year | 2nd year |
| --- | --- |
| 5.1 Actively participate in the construction of scientific knowledge, evidencing the presence of interaction, cooperation and evaluation among peers, improving the capacity for questioning, reflection and debate to reach consensus in the resolution of a problem or learning situation.   5.2 Build and produce knowledge through collective work, through analysis, discussion and synthesis and obtaining as a result products represented in reports, posters, presentations, scientific or dissemination articles, etc.  5.3 Debate, in an informed and reasoned way, on the different environmental, social and ethical issues related to the development of the sciences, reaching a consensus on the impact of these advances on society and proposing common creative solutions to the issues raised. | 5.1 Obtain relationships between physical variables, measuring and treating experimental data, determining errors and using graphic representation systems in analog or digital environments.  5.2 Reproduce in laboratories, whether real or virtual, certain physical processes by modifying the variables that condition them, considering the principles, laws or theories involved, generating the corresponding report in an appropriate format and including arguments, conclusions, tables of data, graphics and bibliographic references.  5.3 Assess the contributions of physics to society, debating in a reasoned way about its impact from the point of view of ethics and sustainability, and reflecting on the causes and consequences of gender bias in the sciences. |

The natural sciences have an intrinsic experimental character. One of the main objectives of any of these scientific disciplines is the explanation of natural phenomena, which makes it possible to formulate theories and laws for their application to different systems. The case of physics is no different, and it is important to transfer students' curiosity about the phenomena that occur in their environment and on different scales. There are everyday physical processes that are easily reproducible and can be explained and described on the basis of the principles and laws of physics. There are also processes that, even if they are not reproducible, are present in the natural environment in a generalized way and thanks to virtual laboratories they can be simulated to approach the study more easily.

Experimental work constitutes a set of stages that encourage collaboration and the exchange of information, which are very necessary in today's research fields. For this reason, it is necessary to encourage experimentation and the estimation of errors, the use of different documentary sources in several languages ​​as well as the skillful and rigorous use of available technological resources. Finally, it is necessary to translate the information into reports that include this entire process.

**Competition 6**

**Justify the multidisciplinary nature of physics and its historical contribution to the advancement of scientific knowledge, to act as critical agents in the analysis and dissemination of information and promote an egalitarian, healthy and sustainable society.**

**Evaluation criteria**

| 1st year | 2nd year |
| --- | --- |
| 6.1 Identify and scientifically argue the repercussions of the actions that the student undertakes in his or her daily life, analyzing how physics can help improve them as a way of actively participating in the construction of an egalitarian, healthy and sustainable society.  6.2 Detect the needs of society on which to apply the appropriate scientific knowledge to help improve it, focusing especially on aspects such as sustainable development and health preservation. | 6.1 Identify the main scientific advances related to physics that have contributed to the laws and theories currently accepted in all scientific disciplines, such as the phases for understanding the methodologies of science, its constant evolution and its universality.   6.2 Recognize the multidisciplinary nature of science and the contributions of some disciplines over others, establishing relationships between physics and other disciplines such as chemistry, biology or mathematics based on contextualized and realistic learning proposals. |

Physics is a science that is deeply involved in different areas of our daily lives and is therefore part of scientific, technological and industrial development. The appropriate application of its principles and laws allows the resolution of various problems based on the same knowledge and the ability to apply in different situations approaches similar to those studied shows the universality of science.

The knowledge and applications of physics form, together with those of other sciences such as mathematics or technology, a symbiotic system where the contributions of each field of knowledge provide a joint benefit. The need to formalize experiments to verify studies implies an incentive in technological development, and vice versa, the progress of technology illuminates new discoveries that need explanation through basic sciences such as physics. Collaboration between different scientific communities, experts in different disciplines, is essential in all this development.

**know**

Knowledge, understood as the set of knowledge, skills, values ​​and attitudes, is formulated in relation to contexts in which competence learning can be developed. Teachers can incorporate alternative contexts if they consider it relevant. In order to facilitate learning and the development of the corresponding specific skills, teachers can assess the possibility of organizing the knowledge of the subject, or of the different subjects coordinated in an area, based on situations.

The situations make it possible to program the course of any level, subject or field from a collection or sequence of challenges, contexts and circumstances of the real world, from which derive questions that need to be answered and that intertwine knowledge, that is, knowledge, skills, values and attitudes, with the capacities that support the competence approach to learning, which modifies the usual planning of the acquisition of knowledge and competences based on academic logic specific to the areas of knowledge or subjects, embodied in the traditional sequence of disciplinary subjects. It aims to approach the learner's logic to give meaning to their learning based on the sequence of relevant contexts embodied in the situations.

**First year**

**Kinematics**

- Analysis, calculation and graphical representation of the temporal evolution of kinematic variables as a function of time in the different movements that an object can have, with or without external forces: resolution of real situations related to physics and the everyday environment.
- Variables that influence rectilinear and circular motion: magnitudes and units used. Qualitative and quantitative analysis of daily movements that present these types of trajectory.
- Description and argumentation of the relationship between the trajectory of a compound movement and the magnitudes that describe it.

**Static and dynamic**

- Prediction, based on the vectorial composition, of the static or dynamic behavior of a particle or a rigid solid.
- Description and argumentation of the relationship between vector mechanics applied to a particle or a rigid solid with its state of rest or motion: static or dynamic applications of physics in other fields, such as engineering or sport.
- Interpretation of the laws of dynamics in terms of quantities such as linear momentum and mechanical impulse: applications in the real world and in contextualized situations (sports, mobility, etc.).

**Energy**

- Concepts of work and power: developing hypotheses about the energy consumption of mechanical or electrical systems in the everyday environment and their performance.
- Calculation of the potential energy and the kinetic energy of a simple system: application to the conservation of mechanical energy in conservative and non-conservative systems and to the study of the causes that produce the movement of objects in the real world.
- Analysis of the thermodynamic variables of a system depending on the conditions: determination of the temperature variations it experiences and the energy transfers that occur with its environment.

**Second year**

**Gravitational Field**

- Determination, through vector calculation, of the gravitational field produced by a system of masses. Effects on the kinematic and dynamic variables of objects immersed in the field.
- Angular momentum of an object in a gravitational field: calculation, relationship with central forces and application of conservation in the study of motion.
- Mechanical energy of an object subjected to a gravitational field: deduction of the type of movement it possesses, calculation of work or existing energy balances in displacements between different positions, speeds and types of trajectories.
- Laws that are verified in planetary motion and extrapolation to the motion of satellites and celestial bodies.
- Introduction to cosmology and astrophysics as an application of the gravitational field: historical evolution of cosmological theories, involvement of physics in the evolution of astronomical objects, knowledge of the universe and repercussion of research in these areas in industry, technology, economy and society.

**Electromagnetic field**

- Electric and magnetic fields: vector treatment, determination of the kinematic and dynamic variables of free electric charges in the presence of these fields. Description and analysis of natural phenomena and technological applications in which these effects are seen.
- Calculation and qualitative analysis of electric field intensity in discrete and continuous charge distributions and interpretation of electric field flow.
- Calculation and qualitative analysis of the energy of a distribution of static charges. Reasoned description of the quantities that change and remain constant with the displacement of free charges between points of different electric potential.
- Qualitative description and calculation of the intensities of the magnetic fields generated by wires with electric current in different geometric configurations: rectilinear, coils, solenoids or torus.
- Analysis of the effects of the interaction of magnetic fields with free electric charges present in their environment.
- Graphic representation and analysis of electric and magnetic field lines produced by simple charge distributions, magnets and wires with electric current in different geometric configurations.
- Generation of the electromotive force: analysis of the operation of motors, generators and transformers from systems where a variation of the magnetic flux occurs.

**Vibrations and Waves**

- Study of oscillatory motion: obtaining and describing the temporal evolution of the kinematic variables of an oscillating body and conservation of energy in these systems.
- Wave motion: analysis and obtaining of oscillation graphs as a function of position and time, of the wave equation that describes it and of the relationship with simple harmonic motion. Study of the different types of wave movements in nature.
- Wave phenomena: natural situations and contexts in which different wave phenomena and applications are evident. Main characteristics of sound waves and their qualities. Contextualization in everyday situations (musical instruments, human hearing and voice generation, echolocation, etc.).
- Description of the nature of light based on historical controversies and debates.
- Visible light as an example of an electromagnetic wave. The electromagnetic spectrum and the properties and applications of the various types of electromagnetic waves.
- Analysis of the behavior of light and the formation of images in media and objects with a different refractive index.
- Study of the generation of images in optical systems: thin lenses, plane and curved mirrors and their applications.

**Relativistic, quantum, nuclear and particle physics**

- The limitations of classical physics. Description and application of the principles of relativity, quantum physics and particle physics to the study of the main particles involved in atomic and nuclear physics: properties and interactions. Implications of wave-corpuscle duality and the uncertainty principle. Assessment of the scientific and technological development possible thanks to quantum physics.
- Qualitative and quantitative study of the photoelectric effect as a system of energy transformation and production of electrical potential differences to apply it technologically.
- Study of natural radioactivity: description of the processes and constants involved that allow the calculation of population variation and the activity of radioactive samples. Application in the field of science and health.
