</h2>
<div id="collapseQuimica" class="accordion-collapse collapse" aria-labelledby="headingQuimica" data-bs-parent="#competenciasAccordion">
<div class="accordion-body">

[**Chemistry**](https://xtec.gencat.cat/web/.content/curriculum/batxillerat/curriculum-171-2022/materias-de-modalitat/modalitat-ciencies-i-tecnologia/Quimica.pdf){target="_blank"}

Chemistry is a science, increasingly present in many areas of society, which can provide answers to problems related to very diverse areas, especially in the fields of health and sustainability. In this sense, the applications of science and chemistry in particular can have a positive impact in very diverse areas. Chemistry provides solutions in the world of drugs, materials, energy and water, among others, and generates knowledge and applications to contribute to the achievement of sustainable development goals.

Chemistry is a science that participates in the new fields of knowledge in the scientific and technical field and makes valuable contributions to the interdisciplinary work of fields as relevant today as nanoscience and nanotechnology, space and material sciences and transformation in numerous industrial sectors, with sustainability criteria. Chemistry also contributes valuable conceptual and technical elements to other scientific disciplines, such as life and health sciences, earth and environmental sciences, and engineering.

Chemistry is therefore an engine of progress and its advances are absolutely necessary to achieve a just and progressing globalized world.

The specific skills that are developed in Chemistry classes promote students' interest and ability to understand the world and intervene in it, and also the assessment of the relevance of this versatile science based on the knowledge of its applications in different contexts. Learning this science helps students prepare for current and future challenges, and become citizens with critical thinking to live, coexist, argue, decide and act based on knowledge.

Chemistry courses at high school actively contribute to each student acquiring a rich and quality scientific cultural base to be a person prepared to live in a society that demands scientific and technical profiles for research and for the world of work, at the same time as it enables a specialization of learning that definitively shapes the personal and professional profile of each student in accordance with what will be their preferences for the future.

The integrative approach in the scientific-technological and mathematical field of the subject of Chemistry prepares students with the scientific knowledge necessary to identify and value the advances aimed at achieving the objectives of sustainable development.

Through the study of chemistry, it is achieved that students develop skills to explain and argue the composition and nature of matter and how it transforms in order to acquire the appropriate theoretical and practical content, with the dual purpose of developing an interest in chemistry and facilitating continuity towards related studies, if the student so desires.

This subject must help train students to effectively manage information in the processes of selection, reworking and construction of knowledge. The approach adopted must enable students to apply the knowledge developed in an integrated way, either in the production of texts that respond to a specific format and situation, using the specific language of chemistry correctly, or in the design of experimental research applied to the verification of a hypothesis, or the development of solutions to problems applied in various contexts, etc. In the same way, the subject must make it possible for students, based on the learning developed and the ability to argue, with logical and ethical criteria, to adopt a suitably justified position and make coherent decisions when faced with a social, political, economic, environmental, health or scientific problem.

The curricular design of the subject is based on specific skills, the development of which gives students the ability to develop knowledge, skills and advanced scientific attitudes. In this sense, the experimental nature of Chemistry must be kept in mind, and for this reason the use of experimental methodologies and tools is proposed, including the mathematical formulation of laws and principles, the appropriate and skillful use of measuring and data collection instruments, whether analog or digital, and all other resources that can facilitate the understanding of chemical concepts and phenomena.

Part of the specific competences of this subject is the ability to know how to elaborate explanations of the foundations of chemical processes and phenomena, to interpret how the models and laws of chemistry work, and to use appropriately the various languages ​​of representation of chemistry, and also to recognize the importance of chemistry and its relationships with other areas of knowledge, the development of working techniques specific to scientific thinking and the repercussions of chemistry in the industrial, health, economic and environmental contexts of society.

Finally, the skills also aim to encourage teamwork, similar to the normal functioning of the scientific community, to become committed people who use science for lifelong learning, for environmental development, for community good and for progress towards an egalitarian, healthy and sustainable society.

Competences must be worked on from learning situations, in real or meaningful contexts, that invite students to reflect, collaborate and take action.

The achievement of the specific skills constitutes the basis for the student's competence assessment and will be assessed through the assessment criteria. There is no univocal and direct link between assessment criteria and knowledge. Specific skills will be assessed by putting different knowledge into action, in different situations, providing the necessary flexibility to establish connections with each other. In a competence approach, the evaluation criteria and knowledge are organized around specific competences.

Accompanying the specific skills of this subject are the assessment criteria, directly linked to the specific skills, which explain the assessment of the skills and knowledge that need to be developed, measure the degree of development of these skills and specify the learning we want to identify in the students and the way to do it. Their character is markedly competitive and makes them evaluators not only of theoretical content, but also of the skills and attitudes that students must acquire in order to develop in a society that demands a critical spirit both in the face of scientific questions and others of a social nature, in which science plays an important role. The teaching staff must contextualize and make these criteria more flexible in accordance with the circumstances of their activity.

The development of specific skills is based on key skills and subject knowledge, which are structured in blocks that include essential knowledge, skills and attitudes. For this reason, it is chosen to formulate the knowledge linked to a capacity and in a context in which they must be developed. The teaching staff can develop an alternative context, if they consider it appropriate.

The different blocks of knowledge in the subject of Chemistry are focused on completing and relating the teachings of previous stages, so that students can acquire a global perception of the different lines of work in chemistry and the various applications.

In the first year of high school, in the block *chemical bond and structure of matter* the study of the structure of matter and chemical bond is studied in depth. The *chemical reactions* blog covers tools for performing advanced stoichiometric calculations and calculations in general with important physicochemical systems such as solutions and ideal gases. In the next block, *organic chemistry*, the knowledge of the previous stage is completed by deepening the general properties of carbon compounds, the typology and nomenclature, the main natural resources that contain them and some of their applications.

In the second year, the knowledge is structured in three large blocks, which coincide with those of the first year. Although they are presented in this document with a prefixed order, there is no defined sequence for the blocks, and thus the distribution throughout a school year allows flexibility in timing, in the methodology and in the relationship with the appropriate contexts to link them to knowledge. In the *chemical bond and structure of matter* block, atomic spectra and the quantum principles of atomic structure are discussed, among others. In the block *chemical reactions* chemical thermodynamics, chemical equilibrium, acid-base reactions and redox are discussed. Finally, the block *organic chemistry* deals with isomerism, organic reactivity and polymers.

This Chemistry curriculum is presented as an integrative proposal that reinforces the foundations of the study, highlighting competency-based learning. Combined with an integrative methodology within the scientific, technological and mathematical environment, it favors meaningful student learning, and should contribute to revealing scientific vocations in a greater number of students, while reducing gender bias.

In the subject of Chemistry, experimental activity is absolutely necessary, so that students are able to ask themselves questions and propose answers through the design and preparation of experiments. This activity, like the rest of the activities that take place in the classroom and are proposed to the students, must be connected to the reality of the students, to give meaning to the learning, in a way that makes visible the interdisciplinary nature of the sciences. For this reason, the proposed methodology is the use of learning situations that connect with real contexts, in order to contribute to the development of key skills on the part of the students and thus achieve a remarkable expansion of their academic, professional, social and personal horizons.

**Specific skills**

**Competition 1**

**Analyze phenomena and solve problems based on situations related to chemistry by using its models, laws and theories, attending to the experimental basis and conceptualization, to evidence the importance of chemistry as a relevant science, and the connections with everyday life, common well-being and environmental sustainability.**

**Evaluation criteria**

| 1st year | 2nd year |
| --- | --- |
| 1.1 Apply models, laws and scientific theories in the analysis of everyday physicochemical phenomena, interpreting the causes that produce them and explaining them using a variety of supports and media.  1.2 Solve physicochemical problems based on everyday situations, applying models, laws and scientific theories to propose and argue possible solutions, expressing the results appropriately.  1.3 Identify problematic situations in the everyday environment, local or global, take initiatives and look for sustainable solutions from chemistry, critically analyzing the impact produced on society and the environment. | 1.1 Recognize the importance of chemistry and its connections with other areas in the development of society, the progress of science, technology, the economy and sustainability, identifying the advances in the field of chemistry that have been fundamental in these aspects.  1.2 Describe the main chemical processes that occur in the environment and the properties of material systems based on the knowledge, skills and attitudes specific to the different disciplines of chemistry.  1.3 Recognize the experimental and interdisciplinary nature of chemistry and its influence in scientific research and in the current economic and labor fields and its applications in other fields of knowledge and human activity. |

The development of this competence requires knowledge of the forms and standard procedures used in the scientific research of the natural world and allows students, in turn, to form an informed opinion on the aspects that affect their immediate reality in order to act with a critical sense in its improvement through scientific knowledge. It makes it possible to detect problems in the everyday environment and address them from the perspective of chemistry, looking for sustainable solutions that have an impact on common social well-being.

With specific competence, it is intended that students also understand that chemistry is a living science, the repercussions of which have not only been important in the past, but also lead to an important contribution to the improvement of present and future society. Through the different branches of chemistry, students will be able to discover which are their most relevant contributions to technology, the economy, society and the environment.

**Competition 2**

**Formulate questions and hypotheses and contrast them through inquiry and experimentation in accordance with safety standards, and argue using models and laws of chemistry in situations related to material systems and the practical applications of chemistry to propose solutions to socio-environmental problems.**

**Evaluation criteria**

| 1st year | 2nd year |
| --- | --- |
| 2.1 Formulate and contrast hypotheses as responses to different problems and observations, using appropriately experimental work, inquiry, the search for evidence and logical-mathematical reasoning.  2.2 Use different methods to find the answer to a single question or observation, comparing the results obtained by different methods and ensuring their consistency and reliability.  2.3 Integrate known laws and scientific theories in the procedure for contrasting the formulated hypotheses, applying qualitative and quantitative relationships between the different variables, to guarantee their reliability and consistency with scientific knowledge.  2.4 Put into practice the knowledge acquired in scientific experimentation in the laboratory, in the field or in other environments, including knowledge of materials and measuring devices and data collection and processing, the basic regulations and safety standards specific to these spaces, and understanding the importance of safety in scientific and entrepreneurial progress. | 2.1 Relate chemistry to current problematic situations, associated with the development of science and technology, analyzing how it is presented through the media or how they are perceived in everyday life.  2.2 Recognize and communicate that chemistry constitutes an essential body of knowledge for the study and discussion of significant issues in the social, economic, political and ethical fields, identifying its presence and influence.  2.3 Apply the models and laws of chemistry in an informed, coherent and reasoned way, explaining and predicting the consequences of experiments, natural phenomena, industrial processes and scientific discoveries.  2.4 Put into practice the knowledge acquired in scientific experimentation in the laboratory, in the field or in other environments, including knowledge of materials and measuring devices and data collection and processing, the basic regulations and safety standards specific to these spaces, and understanding the importance of safety in scientific and entrepreneurial progress. |

This specific competence contributes to ensure that students are able to investigate natural phenomena through experimentation, the search for evidence and scientific reasoning, making use of the knowledge they acquire in their training, using the scientific methodology with more rigor and obtaining more comprehensive and better elaborated conclusions and answers. The questions they raise and the hypotheses they formulate are elaborated in accordance with grounded knowledge and highlight the relationships between the variables. It also contributes to making good use of the safety regulations of scientific laboratories.

Students must be able to identify the basic principles of chemistry that justify that material systems have certain properties and applications in accordance with their composition and that there is a fundamental chemical basis at the bottom of each of the current environmental issues and also in the ideas and methods to solve related problems. In this way, it will be possible to find answers and effective solutions to real and practical issues, as they are presented through our perception or as they are formulated in the media.

**Competition 3**

**Interpret and organize information in different formats from various sources, using appropriately the various chemistry communication registers (units, formulation, symbolic, mathematical language and others), to demonstrate the need to establish a communication tool between scientific communities and in research.**

**Evaluation criteria**

| 1st year | 2nd year |
| --- | --- |
| 3.1 Use and relate rigorously the International System of Units (SI) and other systems of units, using their notation and equivalences correctly, while making effective communication with the entire scientific community possible.  3.2 Name and formulate correctly simple substances, ions and inorganic and organic chemical compounds using IUPAC rules, as part of an integrative and universal language for the entire scientific community.  3.3 Use different formats to interpret and express information related to a specific physicochemical process, relating and extracting the most relevant information from each format for solving a problem.  3.4 Put into practice the knowledge acquired in scientific experimentation in the laboratory, in the field or in other environments, including knowledge of materials and measuring devices and data collection and processing, the basic regulations and safety rules specific to these spaces, and understanding the importance of safety in scientific and entrepreneurial progress. | 3.1 Correctly use the International System of Units (SI) and other unit systems and the IUPAC nomenclature rules as the basis of a universal language for chemistry, which allows effective communication with the entire scientific community.  3.2 Rigorously use mathematical tools to support the development of scientific thinking, applying these tools in solving problems, using equations, units and operations.  3.3 Practice and ensure compliance with the safety rules related to the handling of chemical substances in the laboratory and in other environments, and the procedures for the correct management and disposal of waste, using correctly the communication codes characteristic of chemistry. |

The development of this competence at this educational stage aims for the students to understand the information provided to them about the physico-chemical phenomena that occur in the everyday world, whatever the format in which it is provided to them, and to also produce new information with correctness, truthfulness and fidelity, using correctly the mathematical language, the unit systems, the IUPAC rules and the safety regulations of scientific laboratories, in order to recognize the universal value of the scientific language in the transmission of knowledge that it is needed for the construction of a better society.

The correct use of the universal scientific language and the ease with which to interpret and produce information of a scientific nature allow each student to create constructive relationships between physics, chemistry and the other scientific and non-scientific disciplines typical of other areas of knowledge studied at high school. In addition, it prepares students to establish connections with an active scientific community, concerned with achieving an improvement in society that has an impact on such important aspects as the conservation of the environment and individual and collective health, which gives this specific competence an essential character for this curriculum. This specific competence entails a very important support for science in general, and for chemistry in particular.

**Competition 4**

**Select and critically evaluate information and resources, in different formats and platforms, both in individual and collective work, create and communicate knowledge effectively and in various formats and argue for the responsible use of chemical substances and processes for the recognition of the positive influence of chemistry in society.**

**Evaluation criteria**

| 1st year | 2nd year |
| --- | --- |
| 4.1 Interact with other members of the educational community, through different learning environments, real and virtual, using autonomously and efficiently various analog and digital resources, rigorously and respectfully and critically analyzing all contributions.  4.2 Manage independently and versatilely, individually and in groups, the information and the creation of content, with a scientific basis, using with judgment and rigor the most reliable sources and tools, thus improving personal and collective learning. | 4.1 Analyze the chemical composition of the material systems found in the immediate environment, in the natural environment and in the industrial and technological environment, arguing that their properties, applications and benefits are based on the principles of chemistry.  4.2 Argue in an informed way, applying the theories and laws of chemistry, that the negative effects of certain substances on the environment and on health are due to the misuse of these products or negligence, and not to chemical science itself.  4.3 Explain, using appropriate scientific knowledge, what are the benefits of the many products of chemical technology and how their use and application have contributed to the progress of society. |

The development of scientific skills, and this in particular, requires access to the diversity of information sources for the selection and use of didactic resources, both traditional and digital. Currently, many of the resources needed for teaching and learning chemistry can be found on different digital content platforms, so their autonomous use facilitates the development of higher-level cognitive processes and promotes understanding, making judgments, creativity and personal development. This competence is related to the critical and efficient use and the ability to select the most suitable resources according to the objectives, citing their sources, and the acquisition of autonomy and skill in communication tools for collaborative work.

On the other hand, this competence must contribute to the recognition of the positive influence of chemistry in society, and avoid the pejorative meaning of the word "chemistry", so rooted in our society, and the result of the lack of contrasting information, and of a scientific literacy and specifically in chemistry. The competition must also contribute to developing the ability to argue about the benefits that the progress of chemistry has had on the well-being of society.

**Competition 5**

**Solve and interpret problems in contexts related to chemistry, applying skills of cooperation, coordination, entrepreneurship and work techniques specific to the chemical community (experimentation, inquiry, logical-mathematical reasoning, etc.), to recognize the role of chemistry and predict the influence of its advances in a society based on ethical and sustainable values.**

**Evaluation criteria**

| 1st year | 2nd year |
| --- | --- |
| 5.1 Actively participate in the construction of scientific knowledge, evidencing the presence of interaction, cooperation and evaluation among peers, improving the capacity for questioning, reflection and debate in reaching consensus in the resolution of a problem or a learning situation.  5.2 Build and produce knowledge through collective work, in addition to exploring alternatives to overcome the assimilation of knowledge already elaborated and finding moments for analysis, discussion and synthesis, obtaining as a result the elaboration of products represented in reports, posters, presentations, articles, etc.  5.3 Debate, in an informed and reasoned manner, on the different environmental, social and ethical issues related to the development of the sciences, reaching a consensus on the consequences of these advances and proposing common creative solutions to the issues raised. | 5.1 Recognize the important contribution to chemistry of collaborative work between specialists from different scientific disciplines highlighting the connections between the laws and theories specific to each discipline.  5.2 Recognize the contribution of chemistry to the development of scientific thinking and to the autonomy of critical thinking through the implementation of the work methodologies specific to the scientific disciplines.  5.3 Assess the contributions of physics to society, debating in a reasoned way about its impact from the point of view of ethics and sustainability, and reflecting on the causes and consequences of gender bias in the sciences.  5.4 Solve problems related to chemistry and study situations related to this science, recognizing the importance of the particular contribution of each team member and the diversity of thought, and consolidating positive social skills in work teams.  5.5 Efficiently represent and visualize the most difficult chemistry concepts using digital tools and varied resources, including real and virtual laboratory experiences. |

This competence implies that students develop an attitude committed to experimental work and the development of team research projects, that they adopt certain ethical positions and social commitment. It also involves active work integrated with reading, writing, speaking, technology and mathematics. This work makes much more sense if it is carried out in collaboration within a diverse group that respects differences in gender, orientation, ideology, etc. The ideas that are raised are validated through argumentation, in the same way as in the scientific community, where consensus is a requirement for the universal acceptance of new ideas and discoveries. The positive interdependence between team members, complementarity, shared responsibility, etc. should be highlighted.

In all scientific activity, collaboration between different individuals and entities is essential to achieve scientific progress. Working in a team, fluently using digital tools and varied resources and sharing the results of studies has an impact on a remarkable growth of scientific research, since progress is cooperative. That there is a firm commitment to the improvement of scientific research, with men and women who want to dedicate themselves to it by vocation, is very important for our current society, since it involves the improvement of the quality of life, technology and health, among others.

This specific competence favors the development of work in students in accordance with the basic principles that are put into practice in the experimental sciences and an affinity for the entities and for the people who are dedicated to them and who work to overcome inequalities of gender, orientation, belief, etc. At the same time, by acquiring skills in the use of scientific reasoning, students develop the ability to interpret and solve problematic situations in different contexts of research, the world of work and their everyday reality.

**Competition 6**

**Build chemical knowledge in an active, collective and evolutionary way from situations in the immediate or global environment, and argue the multidisciplinary and versatile nature of chemistry and its relationships with other fields of knowledge to act as critical agents in the analysis and dissemination of information and promote an egalitarian, healthy and sustainable society.**

**Evaluation criteria**

| 1st year | 2nd year |
| --- | --- |
| 6.1 Identify and scientifically argue the repercussions of the actions that the student undertakes in his or her daily life, and analyze how to improve them as a way of actively participating in the construction of a better society.  6.2 Detect the needs of society on which to apply the appropriate scientific knowledge to help improve it, focusing especially on important aspects such as sustainable development and health preservation. | 6.1 Explain and reason the fundamental concepts that are at the base of chemistry by applying the concepts, laws and theories of other scientific disciplines (especially physics) through experimentation and inquiry.  6.2 Deduce the fundamental ideas of other scientific disciplines (for example, biology or technology) by means of the relationship between their basic contents and the laws and theories that are specific to chemistry.  6.3 Solve problems and questions that are characteristic of chemistry using the tools provided by mathematics and technology, thus recognizing the relationship between experimental and natural phenomena and concepts specific to this discipline. |

This specific competence aims to develop in students the ability to decide with scientifically based criteria to be able to assess the technical, social, economic and environmental impact of the different applications of the advances, research and discoveries made by the scientific community over the course of history, with the aim of building competent citizens committed to the world in which they live. This knowledge makes it possible to critically assess the repercussions they have, and encourages students to make decisions about the appropriate uses of scientific and technological media and products.

Likewise, this specific competence is developed through the active participation of students in projects that involve decision-making and the execution of scientifically based actions in their daily lives and in their social environment. This improves the social awareness of science, which is necessary to build a more advanced knowledge society.

It is not possible to deeply understand the fundamental concepts of chemistry without knowing the laws and theories of other fields of science related to it. In the same way, you need to apply the basic ideas of chemistry to understand the foundations of other scientific disciplines. The contributions of chemistry contribute to the development of other sciences and fields of knowledge (and vice versa) and are essential for the global progress of science, technology and society.

In order for students to become competent, they will develop their learning through experimental study and observation of situations in which this interdisciplinary relationship is highlighted, the application of technological tools in inquiry and experimentation, and the use of mathematical tools and logical reasoning in solving chemistry-specific problems. This interdisciplinary and holistic basis is inherent in chemistry and provides the students who study it with adequate foundations so that they can continue their studies in different branches of knowledge, and through different training itineraries, which contributes efficiently to the training of competent people for society.

**know**

Knowledge, understood as the set of knowledge, skills, values ​​and attitudes, is formulated in relation to contexts in which competence learning can be developed. Teachers can incorporate alternative contexts if they consider it relevant. In order to facilitate learning and the development of the corresponding specific skills, teachers can assess the possibility of organizing the knowledge of the subject, or of the different subjects coordinated in an area, based on situations.

The situations make it possible to program the course of any level, subject or field from a collection or sequence of challenges, contexts and circumstances of the real world, from which derive questions that need to be answered and that intertwine knowledge, that is, knowledge, skills, values and attitudes, with the capacities that support the competence approach to learning, which modifies the usual planning of the acquisition of knowledge and competences based on academic logic specific to the areas of knowledge or subjects, embodied in the traditional sequence of disciplinary subjects. It aims to approach the learner's logic to give meaning to their learning based on the sequence of relevant contexts embodied in the situations.

**First year**

**Chemical bond and structure of matter**

- Identification and argumentation of the development of the periodic table: recognition and assessment of the historical contributions in its preparation and of the importance as a predictive tool of the properties of the elements and of the relationship with their daily uses and the problems associated with the current increase in demand for any of them.
- Organization of the electronic structure of atoms and analysis of the interaction with electromagnetic radiation: explanation of the position of an element in the periodic table and the similarity in the properties of the chemical elements of each group in real situations.
- Application of theories on the stability of atoms and ions: prediction of the formation of bonds between the elements, their representation and the prediction of the properties of chemical substances in relation to everyday life. Properties-structure relationship. Verification through observation and experimentation.
- Use of the nomenclature of simple substances, ions and inorganic chemical compounds: relationship with the composition, properties, structure of the substances and their applications in everyday life.

**Chemical Reactions**

- Interpretation and application of the fundamental laws of chemistry: stoichiometric relationships in chemical reactions and in the composition of compounds. Solving quantitative questions related to chemistry in everyday life and/or in socially relevant contexts.
- Identification and classification of chemical reactions: relationships between chemistry and some important aspects of today's society such as, for example, environmental conservation or drug development. Identification and investigation of chemical reactions in everyday life such as acid-base reactions and redox reactions such as combustion.
- Calculation of quantities of matter in specific physicochemical systems, such as ideal gases or solutions, and investigation and interpretation of their properties and the measurable variables of their state in situations of everyday life and in socially relevant contexts.
- Application of the stoichiometry of chemical reactions in contexts of applications in the most significant industrial processes of chemical engineering, and environmental parameters such as the ecological or carbon footprint.

**Organic Chemistry**

- Identification and comparison of general physical and chemical properties of organic compounds based on the chemical structures of their functional groups: generalities in the different homologous series and their applications, especially in contexts close to students and in real situations.
- Use of the IUPAC rules to correctly formulate and name some monofunctional and polyfunctional organic compounds (hydrocarbons, oxygenated compounds and nitrogenous compounds), and establish connections with the uses and products where the formulated compounds are found, in relation to everyday life and issues of ecosocial interest.

**Second year**

**Chemical bond and structure of matter**

- Atomic spectra and spectroscopic techniques
	- Characterization of atomic spectra as experimental evidence responsible for the need for the revision of the atomic model. Identification and argumentation of the relevance of spectroscopy in the context of the historical development of the atomic model.
	- Interpretation of the emission and absorption spectra of the elements and their contribution to the knowledge of the Universe. Relationship with the electronic structure of the atom.
	- Use of data from various spectroscopic techniques (UV, IR, NMR, mass spectrometry) in the identification of substances of interest and relevance in everyday life and current socio-scientific issues. Explanation of the bases of its operation.
- Quantum principles of the atomic structure
	- Relationship between the phenomenon of atomic spectra and the quantization of energy. From the Bohr model to the mechano-quantum models: need for an electronic structure at different levels and its connections with basic scientific research and with current scientific and technological advances.
	- Explanations and application of Heisenberg's uncertainty principle and the dual nature of the wave-corpuscle of the electron and the probabilistic nature of the orbital concept.
	- Identification of quantum numbers and application of the Pauli exclusion principle. Construction of the electronic structure of the atom. Use of the Moeller diagram to write the electronic configuration of the most frequent chemical elements in the environment and the human body, and/or the protagonists of real situations in controversy and with socio-environmental impact.
- Periodic table and properties of atoms
	- Argument based on evidence of the experimental nature of the origin of the periodic table. Justification of the periodic law and grouping of the elements on the basis of the properties.
	- Relationships between current atomic theory and observed experimental laws.
	- Predicting the position of an element in the periodic table based on the electronic configuration, and the electronic configuration based on the position of the element, while establishing connections with the characteristics and uses of the everyday substances that contain it.
	- Reasoning based on the data, or based on the charge model of the atom, of periodic trends. Application to the prediction of the values ​​of the properties of the elements of the table from their position.
- Chemical bonding and intermolecular forces
	- Prediction and justification of the type of bond based on the characteristics of the individual elements that make it up in relation to the properties of the substance formed and its presence in everyday life.
	- Interpretation of the energy involved in the formation of molecules, 3D crystal structures and macromolecular structures. Prediction and justification of properties of chemical substances in relation to everyday life and their uses and interest.
	- Application of Lewis structures and RPECV theory to explain and predict geometries of molecular compounds and their polarity in relation to their behavior in everyday environmental phenomena.
	- Application of the Born-Haber cycle and the energy exchanged in the formation of ionic crystals.
	- Application of electronic cloud models to explain the characteristic properties of metallic crystals in metals of prominent use in current situations.
	- Relationships between intermolecular forces and macroscopic properties of molecular compounds. Relationship of properties with structure (geometry and bonding) in substances that intervene in real situations of local or global interest.

**Chemical Reactions**

- Chemical thermodynamics
	- Application of the first principle of thermodynamics: energy exchanges between systems through heat and work in contexts of consumption and energy efficiency.
	- Representation and use of thermochemical equations and calculation of reaction enthalpies. Concept of enthalpy of reaction and application in real situations and contexts such as fuels, living beings, etc. and in relation to problems such as the increase in carbon dioxide emissions. Differentiation between endothermic and exothermic processes.
	- Application of the energy balance between products and reactants by means of Hess's law, by means of standard enthalpy of formation or bond energies, to obtain the enthalpy of a reaction in nearby or current contexts.
	- Application of the second principle of thermodynamics. Entropy as a quantity that affects the spontaneity and irreversibility of chemical processes in recent or current contexts.
	- Calculation of the Gibbs energy of chemical reactions and their spontaneity as a function of the temperature of the system, and interpretation of the results in recent or current contexts.
- Chemical kinetics
	- Elaboration of explanations and predictions based on the theory of collisions as a sub-microscopic scale model of chemical reactions. Concepts of reaction speed and activation energy in recent or current contexts.
	- Elaboration of explanations and predictions based on the influence of reaction conditions on their speed in recent or current contexts.
	- Application of the differential law of the rate of a chemical reaction and calculation of reaction orders from experimental reaction rate data.
- Chemical balance
	- Application and conceptualization of chemical equilibrium as a dynamic process: rate equations and thermodynamic aspects. Expression of the equilibrium constant using the law of mass action. Application in recent or current contexts and of socio-scientific relevance.
	- Calculation of the equilibrium constant of reactions in which the reactants are in different physical states. Relationship between Kc and Kp and solubility product in heterogeneous equilibria and its connection with natural and industrial processes.
	- Application of Le Châtelier's principle and the reaction quotient. Evolution of systems in equilibrium based on the variation of the conditions of concentration, pressure or temperature of the system, and applications in recent or current contexts.
- Acid-base reactions
	- Justification of the acidic or basic nature of a substance based on the theories of Arrhenius and Brønsted and Lowry and their implications in the classification of acids and bases of substances in the everyday environment.
	- Differentiation between strong and weak acids and bases. Calculation of the degree of dissociation in aqueous solution in nearby or current contexts.
	- Calculation and justification of the pH of acidic and basic solutions. Expression of the constants Ka and Kb, in relation to everyday life and in contexts such as cooking, medicines, the environment, etc.
	- Representation and concept of conjugate acid and base pairs. Prediction of the acid or basic character of the solutions in which the hydrolysis of a salt occurs based on situations in the everyday environment.
	- Identification and representation of reactions between acids and bases and stoichiometric calculations in examples from recent or current contexts. Concept of neutralization. Realization of acid-base volumes, the corresponding calculations and reasoning of the results in relation to real situations and in connection with everyday life.
	- Relationship between properties and applications of relevant acids and bases in the industrial and consumer spheres, with particular relevance to the environmental conservation process.
- redox reactions
	- Calculation and application of the oxidation state. Identification of the species that are reduced or oxidized in a reaction based on the variation of the oxidation number in processes of relevance for their everyday life and/or socio-environmental impact.
	- Equalization by the ion-electron method of chemical oxidation-reduction equations in recent or current contexts. Stoichiometric calculations and redox volumes.
	- Application and conceptualization of the standard potential of a redox couple. Spontaneity of chemical and electrochemical processes involving two redox couples in relation to nearby or current contexts.
	- Application of Faraday's laws: amount of electric charge and amounts of substance in an electrochemical process. Stoichiometric calculations in electrolytic cells in recent or current contexts.
	- Identification and calculations in oxidation and reduction reactions in the manufacture and operation of electric batteries, electrolytic cells and fuel cells, and also in the prevention of metal corrosion.

**Organic Chemistry**

- isomerism
	- Use of molecular formulas and developed organic compounds, in relation to their properties, origins or uses. Different types of structural isomerism in compounds in relation to everyday life and/or relevant problems.
	- Use of molecular models or 3D representation techniques of molecules. Spatial isomers of a compound and properties in compounds in relation to everyday life and/or relevant problems.
- Organic reactivity
	- Identification of the main chemical properties of the different organic functions and their properties and chemical reactions, especially in contexts close to the students.
	- Identification of the main types of organic reactions. Products of the reaction between organic compounds and the corresponding chemical equations in relation to substances of special interest and close to the students.
	- polymers
	- Classification of the different formation processes of polymers from the corresponding monomers. Structure and properties.
	- Classification of polymers according to nature, structure and composition. Applications, properties and associated environmental risks.
