<div class="accordion-item">
<h2 class="accordion-header" id="headingRob">
<button class="accordion-button collapsed" type="button" data-bs-toggle="collapse" data-bs-target="#collapseRob" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="collapseRob">
<strong> ♾️ Matemàtiques - Matèries obligatòries de modalitat</strong>
</button>
</h2>
<div id="collapseRob" class="accordion-collapse collapse" aria-labelledby="headingRob" data-bs-parent="#competenciasAccordion">
<div class="accordion-body">

[**Mathematics**](https://xtec.gencat.cat/web/.content/curriculum/batxillerat/curriculum-171-2022/materias-obligatories-de-modalitat/Matematiques.pdf){target="_blank"}

Mathematics constitutes one of the greatest cultural and intellectual achievements of humanity. Throughout history, different cultures have endeavored to describe nature using mathematics and to transmit all the knowledge acquired to future generations. Today, this intellectual heritage acquires a fundamental value, since the great global challenges, such as respect for the environment, energy efficiency or inclusive and sustainable industrialization, which society will have to face, require students who are able to adapt to changing conditions, to learn autonomously, to model situations, to explore new avenues of research and to use technology effectively. Therefore, it is essential for the citizens of the 21st century to use mathematical knowledge and skills, such as reasoning, modelling, computational thinking or problem solving.

The curricular development of Mathematics I and II is oriented towards the achievement of the general objectives of the stage, paying special attention to the development and achievement of the key skills conceptualized in the high school operational descriptors that students must achieve at the end of the stage. Thus, the interpretation of problems and the communication of procedures and results are related to linguistic communication competence and multilingual competence. The sense of initiative and entrepreneurship in establishing a work plan in continuous review and modification is linked to entrepreneurial competence. Making decisions or adapting to situations of uncertainty are specific components of personal and social competence and of learning to learn. The use of digital tools in the processing of information and in solving problems is directly related to digital competence. Reasoning and argumentation, modeling and computational thinking are characteristic elements of STEM competence. The connections established between mathematics and other areas of knowledge, and problem solving in social contexts, are related to civic competence. On the other hand, mathematical knowledge itself as a universal expression of culture contributes to the competence in cultural awareness and expressions.

In continuity with compulsory secondary education, the main axes of the specific competences in Mathematics are the effective understanding of mathematical concepts and procedures, together with the attitudes specific to the mathematical profession, which allow the construction of a solid conceptual base based on problem solving, reasoning and mathematical research, especially focused on the interpretation and analysis of issues of science and technology. The specific skills focus on the processes that best allow students to develop skills such as problem solving, reasoning and argumentation, representation and communication, together with socio-affective skills. For this reason, the following processes are worked on: problem solving, reasoning and testing, connections, communication and representation, in addition to socio-affective development.

Problem solving and mathematical research are two fundamental components in the teaching of mathematics, as they allow the cognitive processes inherent in this area to be used to address and solve situations related to science and technology, developing reasoning, creativity and abstract thinking. The specific skills of problem solving, reasoning and proof, and connections are designed to acquire the processes specific to mathematical research, such as the formulation of questions, the establishment of conjectures, justification and generalization, the connection between different mathematical ideas and the recognition of concepts and procedures specific to mathematics in other areas of knowledge, particularly in science and technology. It is necessary to highlight the instrumental nature of mathematics as a fundamental tool for areas of scientific and technological knowledge.

Other important aspects of mathematics education are communication and representation. The communication process helps give meaning and permanence to ideas by making them public. On the other hand, to understand and use mathematical ideas, the way in which they are represented is essential. Both issues are intimately related, because the choice of one or another way of representing ideas can condition their communication and understanding. For this reason, a single specific competence is included that includes both aspects, focused on the acquisition of communication and representation processes, both concepts and mathematical procedures.

In order to ensure that all students can make use of fundamental mathematical concepts and relationships, and that they also come to experience their beauty and importance, two specific competencies related to the emotional aspect have been included, one from a personal point of view and the other from a social point of view, in relation to cooperative work and the construction of mathematical knowledge. It is intended to contribute in this way to banishing preconceived ideas in society, such as the belief that only those with innate talent can learn, use and enjoy mathematics, or deeply rooted false stereotypes, for example, those related to gender issues.

Competences must be worked on from learning situations, in real or meaningful contexts, that invite students to reflect, collaborate and take action.

The achievement of specific skills will be assessed using the assessment criteria, which focus on putting skills into action rather than memorizing concepts or the routine reproduction of procedures. There is no univocal and direct link between assessment criteria and knowledge. Specific skills will be assessed by putting different knowledge into action, in different situations, providing the necessary flexibility to establish connections with each other. In a competence approach, the evaluation criteria and knowledge are organized around specific competences. Given the nature of the skills, in some cases the gradation of the evaluation criteria between the first and second courses is carried out by means of knowledge.

The evaluation criteria, linked directly to the specific skills, explain the assessment of the skills and knowledge that needs to be developed, measure the degree of development of these skills and specify the learning we want to identify in the students and the way to do it. The teaching staff must contextualize and make these criteria more flexible in accordance with the circumstances of their activity.

Accompanying the specific skills and evaluation criteria is the body of knowledge that integrates knowledge, skills and attitudes. Although throughout basic education (primary education and compulsory secondary education) knowledge has been grouped into blocks called "senses", a set of skills related to domain in the context of numerical, metric, geometric, algebraic, stochastic and socio-affective content, in high school it has been chosen to organize knowledge into four large blocks: *analysis*, *geometry*, *statistics and probability* and *socio-affective*, to establish bridges between the LOE high school content blocks.

In order not to miss the opportunity to also introduce the vision of mathematical education organized in senses in high school, and to follow the evolution of knowledge between basic education and high school, it has been decided that within each large block the senses that appear in basic education are reunited: numerical, measurement, spatial, algebraic, stochastic and socio-affective.

In each block, some senses are more present than others. Thus, the *analysis* block includes knowledge related to three senses: numerical, measuring and algebraic; in the *geometry* block, knowledge related to four senses is included: numerical, measuring, spatial and algebraic; in the block *statistics and probability*, there is knowledge related to numerical sense, measurement and stochastics. It has been chosen to leave the knowledge relating to the socio-emotional sense as the last block, because due to their characteristics, they are knowledge that must be introduced in parallel while working on the more specific knowledge of the blocks specific to Mathematics.

Numerical sense is characterized by the application of knowledge about numbering and calculation in different contexts, and by the development of skills and ways of doing and thinking based on the understanding, representation and flexible use of numbers, mathematical objects formed by numbers and operations.

The sense of measurement focuses on the understanding and comparison of attributes of objects in the world around us, as well as on the measurement of uncertainty.

Spatial sense addresses the understanding of the geometric aspects of our environment; identifying relationships with each other, placing them, classifying them or reasoning with them are fundamental elements of learning geometry.

The algebraic sense provides the language in which mathematics is communicated; seeing the general in the particular, recognizing dependent relationships between variables and expressing them through different representations, as well as modeling mathematical or real-world situations with symbolic expressions are fundamental characteristics of the algebraic sense. Computational thinking and modeling have been incorporated into this block, but they should not be interpreted as exclusive to it, but should also be developed in the other blocks of knowledge.

The stochastic sense includes the analysis and interpretation of data, the development of conjectures and decision-making based on statistical information, its critical assessment and the understanding and communication of random phenomena in a wide variety of situations.

Finally, the socio-affective sense involves the acquisition and application of knowledge, skills and attitudes necessary to understand and manage the emotions that appear in the process of learning mathematics, in addition to acquiring strategies for teamwork. This sense should not be worked on in isolation, but throughout the development of the subject.

Mathematics is not a collection of separate and unconnected knowledge, but constitutes an integrated field of knowledge. The set of specific skills, assessment criteria and basic knowledge are designed to constitute a whole that facilitates the approach to simple or complex tasks, individual or collective, within the same body of mathematics or multidisciplinary. The use of digital tools to research, interpret and analyze plays an essential role, since processes and operations that required sophisticated manual methods can now be approached simply by using calculators, spreadsheets, dynamic geometry programs or other specific software, favoring reasoning over rote and routine learning.

**Specific skills**

**Competition 1**

**Modeling and solving problems of everyday life and of various fields of knowledge, including mathematics,** **applying different strategies and forms of reasoning,** **to pose and solve challenges.**

**Evaluation criteria**

| 1st year | 2nd year |
| --- | --- |
| 1.1 Generate models based on situations posed in various contexts, both in everyday life and in the academic field, which allow the situations to be turned into mathematical challenges or problems.  1.2 Use tools and strategies to solve problems or make creative proposals in the situations that have been modelled.  1.3 Obtain solutions and make creative proposals to situations raised in various contexts, both in everyday life and in the academic field. | 1.1 Generate models based on situations posed in various contexts, both in everyday life and in the academic field, which allow the situations to be turned into mathematical challenges or problems.  1.2 Use tools and strategies to solve problems or make creative proposals in the situations that have been modelled.  1.3 Obtain solutions and make creative proposals to situations raised in various contexts, both in everyday life and in the academic field.  1.4 Analyze and evaluate different models, tools and strategies. |

Problem solving and modeling are a fundamental axis in the learning of mathematics, as they are central processes in the construction of mathematical knowledge. Modeling and solving problems in diverse contexts can motivate the learning process and establish a solid cognitive foundation that allows you to build mathematical concepts and experience mathematics as a tool to describe, analyze and expand your understanding of situations in everyday life in science and technology, social sciences or other disciplines.

The development of this competence entails the processes of problem formulation, systematization in the search for relevant data or objects and their relationships, their codification in mathematical language or a language that is easy to interpret by a computer system, the creation of abstract models of everyday situations, the use of heuristic resolution strategies such as analogy with other problems, estimation, trial and error, resolution in an inverse way, decomposition into simpler problems, etc.

**Competition 2**

**Arguing the suitability of solutions to a problem, using reasoning and mathematical logic, to verify their validity.**

**Evaluation criteria**

| 1st year | 2nd year |
| --- | --- |
| 2.1 Express with scientific coherence ideas and reasoning that allow to justify the validity of solutions, processes and conclusions.  2.2 Construct and express with scientific coherence texts with mathematical arguments that allow critical judgments to be made or technological, social, artistic and cultural decisions to be made in a sustainable, ethical and environmentally friendly context, in relation to the situation or the problem raised. | 2.1 Express with scientific coherence ideas and reasoning that allow to justify the validity of solutions, processes and conclusions.  2.2 Construct and express with scientific coherence texts with mathematical arguments that allow critical judgments to be made or technological, social, artistic and cultural decisions to be made in a sustainable, ethical and environmentally friendly context, in relation to the situation or the problem raised. |

The analysis of the solutions obtained in the resolution of a problem enhances critical reflection, reasoning and argumentation. The interpretation of the solutions and conclusions obtained considering different perspectives such as sustainability, responsible consumption, equity or non-discrimination, among others, help to make reasoned decisions, evaluate strategies and communicate effectively.

The development of this competence involves reflexive processes typical of metacognition such as the act and co-evaluation, the effective use of digital tools, the verbalization or description of the process and the selection between different ways of checking solutions or strategies to validate the solutions and their scope.

**Competition 3**

**Formulate conjectures or problems, using reasoning and argumentation, creativity and technological tools, to generate new mathematical knowledge.**

**Evaluation criteria**

| 1st year | 2nd year |
| --- | --- |
| 3.1 Ask questions in various contexts that can be answered through mathematical knowledge.  3.2 Make mathematical conjectures autonomously and reasoned in a context in which students have creative freedom making use, if necessary, of technological tools (programming languages, spreadsheets, GeoGebra, mathematical photography, video, etc.).  3.3 Propose problems autonomously, creatively and reasoned in a context in which students have creative freedom making use, if necessary, of technological tools (programming languages, spreadsheets, GeoGebra, mathematical photography, video, etc.). | 3.1 Ask questions in various contexts that can be answered through mathematical knowledge.  3.2 Make mathematical conjectures autonomously and reasoned in a context in which students have creative freedom making use, if necessary, of technological tools (programming languages, spreadsheets, GeoGebra, mathematical photography, video, etc.).  3.3 Propose problems autonomously, creatively and reasoned in a context in which students have creative freedom making use, if necessary, of technological tools (programming languages, spreadsheets, GeoGebra, mathematical photography, video, etc.). |

The formulation of conjectures and the generation of questions of mathematical content are two important and meaningful components of the Mathematics curriculum and are considered an essential part of mathematical learning. Forming conjectures or generating questions with mathematical content about a problematized situation or about a problem already solved involves the creation of new problems with the aim of exploring a given situation, as well as the reformulation of a problem during the resolution process.

The development of this competence can encourage more diverse and flexible thinking, improve the skill to solve problems in various contexts and establish bridges between concrete situations and mathematical abstractions, expand the perception of mathematics and enrich and consolidate concepts. When students generate questions, they improve reasoning and reflection at the same time as they build their own knowledge, translating into a high level of commitment and curiosity, as well as enthusiasm towards the process of learning mathematics.

**Competition 4**

**Use computational thinking by modifying, creating and generalizing strategies and algorithms with digital support to model and solve situations in everyday life or in various fields of knowledge, including mathematics.**

**Evaluation criteria**

| 1st year | 2nd year |
| --- | --- |
| 4.1 Break down a problem or a situation in everyday life into different parts, tackling them one at a time to be able to find the overall solution with digital devices.  4.2 Recognize patterns, similarities and trends in the problems or situations to be solved.  4.3 Find the principles that generate the patterns of a problem by discarding irrelevant data while identifying the most important parts.  4.4 Generate step-by-step instructions to solve a problem and similar ones by testing and carrying out possible solutions with programming languages ​​or with spreadsheets, GeoGebra and mobile application developers among others. | 4.1 Break down a problem or a situation in everyday life into different parts, tackling them one at a time to be able to find the overall solution with digital devices.  4.2 Recognize patterns, similarities and trends in the problems or situations to be solved.  4.3 Find the principles that generate the patterns of a problem by discarding irrelevant data while identifying the most important parts.  4.4 Generate step-by-step instructions to solve a problem and similar ones by testing and carrying out possible solutions with programming languages ​​or with spreadsheets, GeoGebra and mobile application developers among others. |

Computational thinking is directly related to problem solving and the formulation of procedures, using abstraction to identify the most relevant aspects, and the decomposition into simpler tasks with the aim of arriving at a solution to the problem that can be executed by a computer system. Bringing computational thinking to everyday life and to the field of science and technology entails relating the fundamental aspects of computer science to the modeling and simulation needs of students.

The development of this competence entails the creation of abstract models of everyday situations and the field of science and technology, their automation and modeling and their codification in a language that is easy to interpret by a computer system.

**Competition 5**

**Connect different mathematical ideas, establishing links between concepts, procedures, arguments and models, to give meaning to mathematical learning and structure it.**

**Evaluation criteria**

| 1st year | 2nd year |
| --- | --- |
| 5.1 Identify links between different mathematical models to have more tools when tackling a challenge.  5.2 Translate between different representations of the same mathematical concept to extract information from one and apply it to the other.  5.3 Apply interconnected mathematical concepts to address a challenge.  5.4 Draw conclusions through an integrated view of mathematics. | 5.1 Identify links between different mathematical models to have more tools when tackling a challenge.  5.2 Translate between different representations of the same mathematical concept to extract information from one and apply it to the other.  5.3 Apply interconnected mathematical concepts to address a challenge.  5.4 Draw conclusions through an integrated view of mathematics. |

Making connections between different mathematical ideas provides a deeper understanding of how different approaches to the same problem can produce equivalent results. Students can use ideas from one context to test or refute conjectures generated in a different context, and by connecting mathematical ideas to them, they can develop a greater understanding of concepts, procedures, and arguments. Perceiving mathematics as a whole involves studying its internal connections and reflecting on them, both those existing between the blocks of knowledge, and between the mathematics of one level or those of different educational stages.

The development of this competence involves linking new mathematical ideas with previous ideas, recognizing and using the connections between mathematical ideas in problem solving, and understanding how some ideas build on others to form an integrated whole.

**Competition 6**

**Link and contextualize mathematics to other areas of knowledge, addressing the situations that arise from it, to model and solve problems and develop critical, creative and innovative capacity in various situations.**

**Evaluation criteria**

| 1st year | 2nd year |
| --- | --- |
| 6.1 Recognize and use the mathematics present in everyday life using the processes inherent in scientific and mathematical research: infer, measure, communicate, classify, predict, etc. in situations that can be addressed in mathematical terms.  6.2 Recognize and use the connections between mathematics and other subjects in situations that can be addressed in mathematical terms.  6.3 Use the creative potential of mathematics to make innovative proposals in scientific, technological, social, artistic and cultural contexts.  6.4 Identify and value the current and historical contribution of mathematics to the progress of humanity, also from a gender perspective, in the face of the challenges posed by today's society.  6.5 Argue mathematically and with a critical spirit about different socio-cultural aspects such as pseudoscience, politics, environment, economy and consumerism, inequalities, traditions and customs, etc. | 6.1 Recognize and use the mathematics present in everyday life using the processes inherent in scientific and mathematical research: infer, measure, communicate, classify, predict, etc. in situations that can be addressed in mathematical terms.  6.2 Recognize and use the connections between mathematics and other subjects in situations that can be addressed in mathematical terms.  6.3 Use the creative potential of mathematics to make innovative proposals in scientific, technological, social, artistic and cultural contexts.  6.4 Identify and value the current and historical contribution of mathematics to the progress of humanity, also from a gender perspective, in the face of the challenges posed by today's society.  6.5 Argue mathematically and with a critical spirit about different socio-cultural aspects such as pseudoscience, politics, environment, economy and consumerism, inequalities, traditions and customs, etc. |

Observing relationships and establishing mathematical connections is a key aspect of mathematical learning, when students increase their knowledge, their skill in using a wide set of representations and access to technology, connections with other areas of knowledge, especially with the sciences, gives them great mathematical power. The connection between mathematics and other areas of knowledge should not be limited to conceptual knowledge, but extended to procedures and attitudes, so that mathematical procedures and attitudes can be transferred and applied to other subjects and contexts.

The development of this competence entails the establishment of connections between ideas, concepts and mathematical procedures and other areas of knowledge, with real life and their application in solving problems in various situations.

**Competition 7**

**Communicate and represent, individually and collectively, mathematical concepts, procedures and results using oral, written, graphic and multimedia language, through different types of supports, including technological ones, to give meaning to knowledge, transfer it and share it.**

**Evaluation criteria**

| 1st year | 2nd year |
| --- | --- |
| 7.1 Show organization when communicating mathematical ideas.  7.2 Use terminology, symbology and mathematical rigor in the communication and representation of mathematics.  7.3 Express mathematical ideas orally with a coherent and precise record.  7.4 Write mathematical texts of all types (descriptive, argumentative, expository, instructive, etc.) with scientific rigor, fluent and coherent reading and in which the use of language and mathematical symbology is precise.  7.5 Design mathematical representations that are capable, on their own, of expressing synthesized mathematical ideas.  7.6 Use artistic and creative expression to communicate, represent and express mathematical ideas and reasoning, such as mathematical photography, mathematical videos, visual works and music.  7.7 Dialogue with peers and debate mathematical ideas to describe, explain and justify reasoning, processes and conclusions. | 7.1 Show organization when communicating mathematical ideas.  7.2 Use terminology, symbology and mathematical rigor in the communication and representation of mathematics.  7.3 Express mathematical ideas orally with a coherent and precise record.  7.4 Write mathematical texts of all types (descriptive, argumentative, expository, instructive, etc.) with scientific rigor, fluent and coherent reading and in which the use of language and mathematical symbology is precise.  7.5 Design mathematical representations that are capable, on their own, of expressing synthesized mathematical ideas.  7.6 Use artistic and creative expression to communicate, represent and express mathematical ideas and reasoning, such as mathematical photography, mathematical videos, visual works and music.  7.7 Dialogue with peers and debate mathematical ideas to describe, explain and justify reasoning, processes and conclusions. |

In the information society, the need for clear and truthful communication, both orally and in writing, is becoming more apparent every day. Interacting with others offers the possibility to exchange ideas and reflect on them, collaborate, cooperate, generate and consolidate new knowledge, making communication an indispensable element in learning mathematics.

Representations of mathematical ideas, concepts and procedures facilitate reasoning and demonstration, are used to examine relationships and test the validity of answers, are naturally present in digital technologies and are at the heart of mathematical communication.

The development of this competence involves expressing facts, ideas, concepts and complex procedures verbally, analytically and graphically, truthfully and precisely, using the appropriate mathematical terminology, giving meaning and permanence to the ideas and making them public.

It also involves increasing the repertoire of mathematical representations and the knowledge of how to use them effectively, emphasizing the ways in which different representations of the same objects can convey different information and showing the importance of selecting representations appropriate to the task.

**Competition 8**

**Develop self-regulation and personal skills that help identify and manage emotions, learning from mistakes and facing situations of uncertainty as an opportunity, to persevere and enjoy the process of learning mathematics.**

**Evaluation criteria**

| 1st year | 2nd year |
| --- | --- |
| 8.1 Identify the own mistakes made in mathematics, discover the conceptual, procedural or strategic elements that cause them and, finally, express in a reasoned way the reason for the mistake.  8.2 Decide and put into practice specific strategies that allow you to avoid the error and overcome the difficulty.  8.3 Persevere in achieving the objectives by implementing new mathematical strategies while identifying and managing one's emotions.  8.4 Actively participate in the self-evaluation, sharing and agreeing with the teaching staff on improvement strategies.  8.5 Develop creative ability by making innovative mathematical proposals related to artistic, cultural, social and technological aspects and enjoying the freedom to decide without showing fear of making mistakes. | 8.1 Identify the own mistakes made in mathematics, discover the conceptual, procedural or strategic elements that cause them and, finally, express in a reasoned way the reason for the mistake.  8.2 Decide and put into practice specific strategies that allow you to avoid the error and overcome the difficulty.  8.3 Persevere in achieving the objectives by implementing new mathematical strategies while identifying and managing one's emotions.  8.4 Actively participate in the self-evaluation, sharing and agreeing with the teaching staff on improvement strategies.  8.5 Develop creative ability by making innovative mathematical proposals related to artistic, cultural, social and technological aspects and enjoying the freedom to decide without showing fear of making mistakes. |

The resolution of more global problems or challenges in which mathematics is involved often represents a challenge that involves a multitude of emotions that the students must manage correctly. Emotional skills in learning mathematics promote students' well-being, emotional regulation and interest in their learning.

The development of this competence entails identifying and managing emotions in the process of learning mathematics, recognizing sources of stress, being persevering in achieving goals, thinking critically and creatively, creating resilience and maintaining a proactive attitude towards new mathematical challenges.

**Competition 9**

**Cooperate, developing the social skills necessary to actively participate in inclusive work teams recognizing the diversity and value of others' contributions, to share and build mathematical knowledge collectively.**

**Evaluation criteria**

| 1st year | 2nd year |
| --- | --- |
| 9.1 Contribute and share strategies and mathematical reasoning with colleagues and value collective success as a strategy for personal improvement.  9.2 Collaborate in teamwork both in face-to-face and virtual environments, listening to others and valuing their contributions, respecting the gender perspective and multiculturalism, sharing and building mathematical knowledge together.  9.3 Ideate, design and contribute mathematical activities and problems of conceptual quality to the rest of the classmates in order to actively participate in the collective construction of mathematical knowledge.  9.4 Help identify mistakes and learning difficulties of colleagues by making constructive and concrete contributions that can help overcome them and improve.  9.5 Use the Catalan language in learning mathematics as a tool for cohesion, inclusion and equity. | 9.1 Contribute and share strategies and mathematical reasoning with colleagues and value collective success as a strategy for personal improvement.  9.2 Collaborate in teamwork both in face-to-face and virtual environments, listening to others and valuing their contributions, respecting the gender perspective and multiculturalism, sharing and building mathematical knowledge together.  9.3 Ideate, design and contribute mathematical activities and problems of conceptual quality to the rest of the classmates in order to actively participate in the collective construction of mathematical knowledge.  9.4 Help identify mistakes and learning difficulties of colleagues by making constructive and concrete contributions that can help overcome them and improve.  9.5 Use the Catalan language in learning mathematics as a tool for cohesion, inclusion and equity. |

Work on the values ​​of respect, tolerance, equality or peaceful resolution of conflicts, at the same time as solving mathematical challenges by developing effective communication skills, planning, inquiry, motivation and trust, to create healthy relationships and work environments, which allow self-confidence to be strengthened and situations of coexistence in equality to be normalized. Likewise, the breakdown of stereotypes and preconceived ideas about mathematics associated with individual issues, such as gender or aptitude for mathematics, must be encouraged.

The development of this competence involves showing empathy for others, establishing and maintaining positive relationships, exercising active listening and assertive communication, working in a team and making responsible decisions.

**know**

Knowledge, understood as the set of knowledge, skills, values ​​and attitudes, is formulated in relation to contexts in which competence learning can be developed. Teachers can incorporate alternative contexts if they consider it relevant. In order to facilitate learning and the development of the corresponding specific skills, teachers can assess the possibility of organizing the knowledge of the subject, or of the different subjects coordinated in an area, based on situations.

The situations make it possible to program the course of any level, subject or field from a collection or sequence of challenges, contexts and circumstances of the real world, from which derive questions that need to be answered and that intertwine knowledge, that is, knowledge, skills, values and attitudes, with the capacities that support the competence approach to learning, which modifies the usual planning of the acquisition of knowledge and competences based on academic logic specific to the areas of knowledge or subjects, embodied in the traditional sequence of disciplinary subjects. It aims to approach the learner's logic to give meaning to their learning based on the sequence of relevant contexts embodied in the situations.

**First year**

***Analysis***

**Number Sense**

- relationships
	- Complex numbers as solutions of polynomial equations within their historical context.

**Sense of measurement**

- change
	- Estimation or calculation of the value of a limit from a table, a graph or an algebraic expression in the context of work with functions to analyze its continuity.
	- Construction of the concept of the derivative of a function based on the study of the change of the function in different contexts.

**Algebraic sense**

- patterns
	- Generalize patterns using explicitly and recursively defined functions.
	- Use spreadsheets or GeoGebra to generalize functions recursively or explicitly.
- Mathematical model
	- Determine the class of function (polynomial, exponential, irrational, rational, logarithmic, trigonometric and piecewise functions) that models quantitative relationships in various contexts: scientific, social and specific to mathematics.
	- Use technological tools to determine the most appropriate functional models in various contexts or to solve the resulting equations.
- Equality and inequality
	- Solving equations, inequalities and systems to find solutions to challenges that arise from the modeling of a situation.
- Relations and functions
	- Analysis, representation and interpretation of quantitative relationships using technological tools when necessary.
	- Study of the properties of various classes of functions: polynomial, exponential, irrational, rational, logarithmic, trigonometric and piecewise functions.
	- Use of symbolic algebra in the representation and explanation of mathematical relationships in different contexts.
- Computational thinking
	- Formulation, resolution and analysis of problems in various contexts with the most appropriate tools and programs.
	- Comparison of alternative algorithms to solve the same problem through logical reasoning.

***Geometry***

**Number Sense**

- Sense of operations
	- Addition and scalar product of vectors in the plane: properties and representations, also using GeoGebra to make the representations.

**Sense of measurement**

- measure
	- Using trigonometric ratios to determine lengths and angle measures in triangle solving problems.

**Spatial Sense**

- Two-dimensional geometric shapes
	- Analysis of the properties and fundamental characteristics of two-dimensional geometric objects.
	- Solving problems related to geometric objects in the plane represented with Cartesian coordinates.
- Location and representation systems
	- Representation and exploration, with the help of digital tools, of the relationships between geometric objects on the plane (geometric transformations, movements on the plane, isometries, congruence and similarity).
	- Selection of the most appropriate algebraic expression to express geometric objects based on the situation to be solved.
- Visualization, reasoning and geometric modeling
	- Representation of geometric objects on the plane using digital tools including the functions and figures that can be formed from a moving point in a geometric location based on its properties.
	- Use of mathematical models (geometric, algebraic, graphs, etc.) in solving problems on the plan linked to contexts connected to other disciplines and areas of interest, including artistic ones.
	- Validation through the deduction and demonstration of geometric theorems and/or conjectures on the plan and verification with digital tools (GeoGebra).
	- Modeling the position and movement of an object in the plane using vectors. Visualization based on parameters (sliding points) with GeoGebra.

**Algebraic Sense**

- Mathematical model
	- Use of matrices and their operations to model movements in the plane (isometries, congruence and similarity).
- Equality and inequality
	- Solving equations, inequalities and systems to find solutions to challenges that arise from the modeling of a situation.
- Relations and functions
	- Use of symbolic algebra in the representation and explanation of mathematical relationships in different contexts.
- Computational thinking
	- Formulation, resolution and analysis of problems in various contexts with the most appropriate tools and programs.
	- Comparison of alternative algorithms to solve the same problem through logical reasoning.

***Probability and Statistics***

**Number Sense**

- counting
	- Use of counting techniques (tree diagrams, permutations, combinations, variations) to solve problems in which elements of a set must be counted.

**Sense of measurement**

- measure
	- Analysis of the uncertainty associated with a random phenomenon by means of probability.

**Sense Stochastic**

- Distribution: organization and analysis of data
	- Organization of data from two-dimensional variables using joint distribution and marginal and conditional distributions. Analysis of statistical dependence.
	- Use and differentiation between linear or quadratic regression for the study of the relationship between two variables, assessing the relevance of the different adjustments.
	- Using the linear correlation coefficient to quantify the linear relationship between two variables. Analysis of their reliability to make predictions in different contexts, in particular scientific and technological ones.
	- Use of the calculator, spreadsheet or specific software in the analysis of statistical data.
- Predictability and uncertainty
	- Calculation of the probability of an event based on the concept of relative frequency.
	- Calculation of probabilities in simple experiments using Laplace's rule in equiprobability situations and in combination with different counting techniques.
- inference
	- Design of statistical studies using digital tools to respond to challenges or problems likely to be treated with statistical methods.
	- Analysis of one-dimensional and two-dimensional samples with technological tools in order to issue judgments and make decisions.

***Social-emotional knowledge***

**Socio-emotional sense**

- Beliefs, attitudes and emotions
	- Self-regulation skills aimed at discovering one's own areas of improvement and personal development.
	- Willingness to delve into certain aspects of mathematical abstraction as the only way to improve its applicability.
	- Perseverance in achieving a goal by exploring and redefining, if necessary, the strategies necessary for personal growth.
	- Creative capacity making innovative mathematical proposals related to artistic, cultural, social and technological aspects in which the enjoyment of doing mathematics is present
	- Ability to identify own conceptual confusions that determine the mistakes made in mathematics, valuing them as an important source of learning.
- Decision making
	- Ability to put into practice concrete strategies that help to overcome own conceptual confusions.
	- Skills to explore and evaluate different strategies in the mathematical treatment of a problem or situation.
	- Skills in improving learning strategies based on suggestions for improvement made in assessments and co-assessments.
	- Ability to make personal decisions based on the critical analysis of a situation that can be treated with mathematical argumentation.
- Inclusion, respect and diversity
	- Ability to listen, respect and try mathematical strategies proposed by another person.
	- Ability to contribute ideas and arguments that help the learning of colleagues.
	- Ability to agree on different opinions and strategies when making a collective decision in the development of a mathematical activity.
	- Appreciation of collective success as an individual success.
	- Appreciation of the contribution of mathematics and the role of mathematicians and mathematics throughout history in multiple aspects that surround us, both in the artistic and cultural, social, scientific and technological fields.

 **Second year**

***Analysis***

**Sense of measurement**

- measure
	- Solving problems involving measurements of length, area or volume in a Cartesian coordinate system.
	- Interpretation of the integral defined as the area under a curve.
	- Calculation of areas under a curve through the calculation of primitives, using elementary techniques.
	- Solving problems involving the calculation of flat surfaces or volumes of revolution, applying the concept of integral.
- change
	- Application of the concepts of limit, continuity and derivability to the representation and study of situations that can be modeled using functions.
	- Use of the derivative as a reason for change in solving optimization problems in various contexts.

**Algebraic Sense**

- Mathematical model
	- Identification of the function class (polynomial, exponential, irrational, rational, logarithmic, trigonometric and piecewise functions) that models quantitative relationships in various contexts: scientific, social and specific to mathematics.
	- Use of technological tools to determine the most appropriate functional models in various contexts or to solve the resulting equations.
- Equality and inequality
	- Solving equations, inequalities and systems to find solutions to challenges that arise from the modeling of a situation.
- Relations and functions
	- Analysis, representation and interpretation of quantitative relationships using technological tools when necessary.
	- Study of the properties of various classes of functions: polynomial, exponential, irrational, rational, logarithmic, trigonometric and piecewise functions.
	- Use of symbolic algebra in the representation and explanation of mathematical relationships in different contexts.
- Computational thinking
	- Formulation, resolution and analysis of problems in various contexts with the most appropriate tools and programs.
	- Comparison of alternative algorithms to solve the same problem through logical reasoning.

***Geometry***

**Sense of measurement**

- measure
	- Solving problems involving measurements of length, area or volume in a Cartesian coordinate system.

**Spatial Sense**

- Geometric shapes of two and three dimensions
	- Three-dimensional geometric objects: analysis of properties and fundamental characteristics.
	- Solving problems related to geometric objects in space represented with Cartesian coordinates.
- Location and representation systems
	- Relationships of geometric objects in space: representation and exploration with the help of digital tools.
	- Algebraic expressions of geometric objects in space: selection of the most appropriate depending on the situation to be solved.
- Visualization, reasoning and geometric modeling
	- Representation of geometric objects in space using digital tools.
	- Use of mathematical models (geometric, algebraic, etc.) to solve problems in space both in the mathematical context and in connection with other disciplines and areas of interest.
	- Validation through deduction and theorem proving of geometric conjectures in space.
	- Modeling the position and movement of an object in space using vectors.

**Algebraic Sense**

- Mathematical model
	- Use of matrices to model situations derived from scientific, social and everyday life contexts.
- Equality and inequality
	- Techniques and use of matrices to model situations in which systems of linear equations appear.
- Relations and functions
	- Use of symbolic algebra in the representation and explanation of mathematical relationships in different contexts.
- Computational thinking
	- Formulation, resolution and analysis of problems in various contexts with the most appropriate tools and programs.
	- Comparison of alternative algorithms to solve the same problem using logical reasoning.

***Probability and Statistics***

**Sense of measurement**

- measure
	- Analysis of the uncertainty associated with a random phenomenon through probability: subjective, classical and frequentist interpretation.

**Sense Stochastic**

- uncertainty
	- Calculation of probabilities in composite experiments. Conditional probability and independence between random events. Tree diagrams and contingency tables.
	- Problem solving and interpretation of Bayes theorem to update probability based on observation and experimentation and decision making under conditions of uncertainty.
- Probability distributions
	- Identification of the different types of discrete and continuous random variables.
	- Use and interpretation of the parameters of a distribution and application to the binomial and normal distributions.
	- Modeling stochastic phenomena using binomial and normal probability distributions. Calculation of associated probabilities using technological tools.

***Social-emotional knowledge***

**Socio-emotional sense**

- Beliefs, attitudes and emotions
	- Self-regulation skills aimed at discovering one's own areas of improvement and personal development.
	- Willingness to delve into certain aspects of mathematical abstraction as the only way to improve its applicability.
	- Perseverance in achieving a goal by exploring and redefining, if necessary, the strategies necessary for personal growth.
	- Creative capacity making innovative mathematical proposals related to artistic, cultural, social and technological aspects in which the enjoyment of doing mathematics is present.
	- Ability to identify own conceptual confusions that determine the mistakes made in mathematics, valuing them as an important source of learning.
- Decision making
	- Ability to put into practice concrete strategies that help to overcome own conceptual confusions.
	- Skills to explore and evaluate different strategies in the mathematical treatment of a problem or situation.
	- Skills in improving learning strategies based on suggestions for improvement made in assessments and co-assessments.
	- Ability to make personal decisions based on the critical analysis of a situation that can be treated with mathematical argumentation.
- Inclusion, respect and diversity
	- Ability to listen, respect and try mathematical strategies proposed by another person.
	- Ability to contribute ideas and arguments that help the learning of colleagues.
	- Ability to agree on different opinions and strategies when making a collective decision in the development of a mathematical activity.
	- Appreciation of collective success as an individual success.
	- Appreciation of the contribution of mathematics and the role of mathematicians and mathematics throughout history in multiple aspects that surround us, both in the artistic, cultural, social, scientific and technological fields.
