<h2 class="accordion-header" id="headingRob">
<button class="accordion-button collapsed" type="button" data-bs-toggle="collapse" data-bs-target="#collapseRob" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="collapseRob">
<strong>♾️ Matemàtiques Generals - Matèries obligatòries de modalitat</strong>
</button>
</h2>
<div id="collapseRob" class="accordion-collapse collapse" aria-labelledby="headingRob" data-bs-parent="#competenciasAccordion">
<div class="accordion-body">

[**General Mathematics**](https://xtec.gencat.cat/web/.content/curriculum/batxillerat/curriculum-171-2022/materias-obligatories-de-modalitat/Matematiques-Generals.pdf){target="_blank"}

The dizzying development of today's world makes it necessary for students to have the ability to analyze and interpret reality in order to adapt to conditions full of uncertainty, in addition to having the necessary skills to learn for themselves. Mathematics plays a fundamental role in modelling, analyzing and understanding the phenomena of multiple fields of knowledge: social, educational, scientific, economic, etc. Mathematical competences include, in addition to mathematical ideas and elements, problem-solving, mathematical reasoning and communication skills, which can be extrapolated to non-mathematical contexts.

The subject of General Mathematics is a compulsory subject within the general modality of the baccalaureate that contributes to the achievement of the general objectives of the stage, paying special attention to the development and achievement of the key skills conceptualized in the operational descriptors of the baccalaureate that students must achieve at the end of the stage. In this modality, the objective of mathematical knowledge must be the application of mathematics for the interpretation and analysis of problematic situations in various real contexts, which make it easier for students to face the challenges of the 21st century as informed and committed citizens.

The fundamental axes that articulate the subject-specific competencies are, in continuity with the compulsory secondary education curriculum, problem solving and the analysis and interpretation of information. In addition, mathematical reasoning and the establishment of connections are addressed, paying special attention in this subject to various non-mathematical contexts, to their relationship with other subjects and to reality, and to mathematical communication.

In order to ensure that all students can make use of fundamental mathematical concepts and relationships, and that they also come to experience the beauty and usefulness of mathematics, banishing preconceived ideas and stereotypes strongly rooted in society, two specific competencies related to the emotional aspect have been included, one from a personal point of view and the other from a social point of view, in relation to cooperative work and the construction of knowledge mathematician

General Mathematics contributes to the development of STEM competence through reasoning and argumentation, modeling and computational thinking. In addition, they favor the search for beauty or harmony, and the description of multiple artistic manifestations such as painting, architecture or music, thus contributing to competition in cultural awareness and expressions. They stimulate the search for entrepreneurial and creative solutions to problems, adding value to entrepreneurial competence. They contribute to the intellectual training of students and to the analysis of social situations, which allows them to develop a critical sense and civic competence. The use of digital tools in the processing of information and in solving problems is directly related to digital competence. Communication plays a central role in mathematical reasoning, as it is necessary for the interpretation of statements and the transmission of results. Finally, the educational value of this subject in terms of personal, social and learning competence should be highlighted, since it provides instrumental tools that allow the construction of new knowledge.

Based on problem solving, reasoning and mathematical representation strategies that are applicable to the diversity of contexts must be provided. Areas such as the economy, environmental balance, science, health or technology must serve to enrich the contexts of the problems formulated. But these too must be based on contexts in areas that are apparently further away from mathematics: linguistics, geography or historical research must also be a source of enrichment. On the other hand, personal and work contexts should not be forgotten as problems related to personal finances or the interpretation of complex numerical information in invoices or advertising brochures. It is important that the links between this subject and other disciplines are explored and analyzed in order to give meaning to concepts and mathematical thinking.

Competences must be worked on from learning situations, in real or meaningful contexts, that invite students to reflect, collaborate and take action.

The evaluation criteria formulated are intended to determine the degree of achievement of the specific skills, which must guide the learning process, so that it is oriented towards putting the skills into action as opposed to the memorization of concepts or the routine reproduction of procedures, so that learning has meaning and is truly meaningful.

There is no univocal and direct link between assessment criteria and knowledge. Specific skills will be assessed by putting different knowledge into action, in different situations, providing the necessary flexibility to establish connections with each other. The achievement of specific skills can be assessed based on the mobilization of various knowledge, which have been distributed in the blocks that have been defined for the curriculum of the areas and subjects of mathematics in the previous stages, called "senses", thus providing coherence to the curriculum as a whole.

The evaluation criteria, linked directly to the specific skills, explain the assessment of the skills and knowledge that needs to be developed, measure the degree of development of these skills and specify the learning we want to identify in the students and the way to do it. The teaching staff must contextualize and make these criteria more flexible in accordance with the circumstances of their activity.

Accompanying the specific skills and evaluation criteria is the body of knowledge that integrates knowledge, skills and attitudes. Although throughout basic education (primary education and compulsory secondary education) knowledge has been grouped into blocks called "senses", a set of skills related to domain in the context of numerical, metric, geometric, algebraic, stochastic and socio-affective content, in high school it has been chosen to organize knowledge into four large blocks: *analysis*, *geometry*, *statistics and probability* and *socio-affective*, to establish bridges between the LOE high school content blocks.

In order not to lose the opportunity to also introduce the vision of mathematical education organized in senses in high school, and to follow the evolution of knowledge between basic education and high school, it has been decided that within each large block the senses that appear in basic education are reunited: numerical, measuring, algebraic, spatial, stochastic and socio-affective.

In the numerical sense, the handling and understanding of numbers is strengthened, advancing in more complex counting techniques, while deepening the understanding of numerical information present in various social and scientific contexts in the form of rates, increments, etc.

In the sense of measurement, the study and analysis of change in different contexts is explored, as well as the measurement of uncertainty.

In the spatial sense, graph theory is introduced, a tool with important applications in the visualization and modeling of problems in various contexts.

In the algebraic sense, we investigate situations and phenomena that can be modeled using equations and functions with the support of technological tools. Computational thinking and modeling have been incorporated into this block, but they should not be interpreted as exclusive to it, but should also be developed in the other blocks of knowledge.

In the stochastic sense, skills in data analysis and interpretation, the handling of uncertainty and the modeling of random phenomena are affirmed. Finally, the knowledge corresponding to the socio-affective sense must be dealt with in an integrated way with those corresponding to the other senses, a matter of particular interest for students studying the general mode of high school. Teamwork must be promoted, accepting diversity and fostering attitudes that respect inclusion and non-discrimination. Learning from mistakes and developing frustration tolerance are especially important at this educational stage. The order of appearance of the senses and the knowledge within them does not entail any sequencing.

The achievement of specific skills and the development of basic knowledge must take into account the new ways of doing and thinking about mathematics. The role currently played by technological tools and the ease of access to increasingly powerful devices are changing the procedures in mathematics. Processes and operations that require sophisticated manual solution methods can now be addressed simply by using calculators, spreadsheets, dynamic geometry programs and other digital tools. This possibility means that teaching can focus on strengthening the concepts and basic attitudes of the subject, and deepening the use of mathematics to interpret and analyze situations and solve problems in different contexts, use simple calculation and measurement instruments, paying less attention to manual and repetitive procedures. In this sense, learning should preferably be oriented towards the interpretation and analysis of phenomena and the acquisition of mathematical reasoning, avoiding practices that involve rote and routine learning.

**Specific skills**

**Competition 1**

**Modeling and solving problems of everyday life and of various fields of knowledge, including mathematics,** **applying different strategies and forms of reasoning** **to pose and solve challenges.**

**Evaluation criteria**

1.1 Generate models based on situations posed in various contexts, both in everyday life and in the academic field, which allow situations to be turned into mathematical challenges or problems.

1.2 Use tools and strategies to solve problems or make creative proposals in the situations that have been modelled.

1.3 Obtain solutions and make creative proposals to the situations raised in various contexts, both in everyday life and in the academic field, for learning mathematics, since they are central processes in the construction of mathematical knowledge.

Modeling and solving problems, both in everyday life and in the different fields of knowledge, in particular that of the social sciences, can motivate the learning process and establish solid cognitive foundations that allow the construction of mathematical concepts and experience mathematics as a tool to describe, analyze and expand the understanding of situations in the everyday life of science and technology, the social sciences or other disciplines.

The development of this competence involves the processes of problem formulation, systematization in the search for relevant data or objects and their relationships, their codification in mathematical language or a language that is easy to interpret by a computer system, the creation of abstract models of everyday situations, the use of resolution strategies such as analogy with other problems, estimation, trial and error, solving it inversely, decomposition into simpler problems, etc.

**Competition 2**

**Argue the suitability of the solutions to a problem using reasoning and mathematical logic to verify their validity.**

**Evaluation criteria**

2.1 Express, with scientific coherence, ideas and reasoning that allow to justify the validity of solutions, processes and conclusions.

2.2 Construct and express scientifically coherent texts with mathematical arguments that allow critical judgments to be made or technological, social, artistic and cultural decisions to be made in a sustainable, ethical and environmentally friendly context, in relation to the situation or the problem at hand.

The analysis of the solutions obtained in the resolution of a problem enhances critical reflection, reasoning and argumentation. The interpretation of the solutions and conclusions obtained considering different perspectives such as sustainability, responsible consumption, equity or non-discrimination, among others, help to make reasoned decisions, evaluate strategies and communicate effectively.

The development of this competence involves reflective processes typical of metacognition, such as the act and co-evaluation, the effective use of digital tools, the verbalization or description of the process and the selection between different ways of checking solutions or strategies to validate the solutions and their scope.

**Competition 3**

**Formulate conjectures or problems, using reasoning and argumentation, creativity and technological tools, to generate new mathematical knowledge.**

**Evaluation criteria**

3.1 Ask questions in various contexts that can be answered using mathematical knowledge.

3.2 Make mathematical conjectures autonomously and reasoned in a context in which students have creative freedom making use, if necessary, of technological tools (programming languages, spreadsheets, GeoGebra, mathematical photography, video, etc.).

3.3 Propose problems autonomously, creatively and reasoned in a context in which students have creative freedom making use, if necessary, of technological tools (programming languages, spreadsheets, GeoGebra, mathematical photography, video, etc.).

Formulating conjectures and generating questions about mathematical content are two important and meaningful components of the mathematics curriculum and are considered an essential part of mathematical learning. Forming conjectures or generating questions with mathematical content about a problematized situation or about a problem already solved involves the creation of new problems with the aim of exploring a given situation, and also the reformulation of a problem during the process of solving it.

The development of this competence can encourage more diverse and flexible thinking, improve the skill to solve problems in various contexts and establish bridges between concrete situations and mathematical abstractions, expand the perception of mathematics, and enrich and consolidate concepts. When students generate questions, they improve reasoning and reflection at the same time as they build their own knowledge, which translates into a high level of commitment and curiosity, and enthusiasm towards the process of learning mathematics.

**Competition 4**

**Use computational thinking by modifying, creating and generalizing strategies and algorithms with digital support to model and solve situations in everyday life or in various fields of knowledge, including mathematics.**

**Evaluation criteria**

4.1 Break down a problem or a situation in everyday life into different parts, tackling them one at a time to be able to find the overall solution with digital devices.

4.2 Recognize patterns, similarities and trends in the problems or situations to be solved.

4.3 Find the principles that generate the patterns of a problem by discarding irrelevant data while identifying the most important parts.

4.4 Generate step-by-step instructions to solve a problem and similar ones by testing and carrying out possible solutions with programming languages ​​or also with spreadsheets, GeoGebra and mobile application developers among others.

Computational thinking is directly related to problem solving and the formulation of procedures, using abstraction to identify the most relevant aspects and decomposition into simpler tasks, with the aim of arriving at a solution to the problem that can be executed by a computer system. Bringing computational thinking to everyday life and to the field of science and technology entails relating the fundamental aspects of computer science to the modeling and simulation needs of students.

The development of this competence entails the creation of abstract models of everyday situations and the field of science and technology, their automation and modeling and their coding in a language that is easy to interpret by a computer system.

**Competition 5**

**Connect different mathematical ideas, establishing links between concepts, procedures, arguments and models, to give meaning to mathematical learning and structure it.**

**Evaluation criteria**

5.1 Identify links between different mathematical models to have more tools when tackling a challenge.

5.2 Translate between different representations of the same mathematical concept to extract information from one and apply it to the other.

5.3 Apply interconnected mathematical concepts to address a challenge.

5.4 Draw conclusions through an integrated view of mathematics.

Making connections between different mathematical ideas provides a deeper understanding of how different approaches to the same problem can produce equivalent results. Students can use ideas from one context to test or refute conjectures generated in a different context, and by connecting mathematical ideas to them, they can develop a greater understanding of concepts, procedures, and arguments. Perceiving mathematics as a whole involves studying its internal connections and reflecting on them, both those existing between the blocks of knowledge, and between the mathematics of one level or those of different educational stages.

The development of this competence involves linking new mathematical ideas with previous ideas, recognizing and using the connections between mathematical ideas in solving problems and understanding how some ideas build on others to form an integrated whole.

**Competition 6**

**Link and contextualize mathematics to other areas of knowledge, addressing the situations that arise from it, to model, solve problems and develop critical, creative and innovative capacity in various situations.**

**Evaluation criteria**

6.1 Recognize and use the mathematics present in everyday life using the processes inherent in scientific and mathematical research: infer, measure, communicate, classify, predict, etc., in situations likely to be addressed in mathematical terms.

6.2 Recognize and use the connections between mathematics and other subjects in situations that can be addressed in mathematical terms.

6.3 Use the creative potential of mathematics to make innovative proposals in scientific, technological, social, artistic and cultural contexts.

6.4 Identify and value the current and historical contribution of mathematics to the progress of humanity, also from a gender perspective, in the face of the challenges posed by today's society.

6.5 Argue mathematically and with a critical spirit about different socio-cultural aspects such as pseudoscience, politics, environment, economy and consumerism, inequalities, traditions and customs, etc.

Observing relationships and establishing mathematical connections is a key aspect of mathematical learning, when students increase their knowledge, their skill in using a wide set of representations and access to technology, connections with other areas of knowledge, especially with the sciences, gives them great mathematical power. The connection between mathematics and other areas of knowledge should not be limited to conceptual knowledge, but extended to procedures and attitudes, so that mathematical procedures and attitudes can be transferred and applied to other subjects and contexts.

The development of this competence entails the establishment of connections between ideas, concepts and mathematical procedures and other areas of knowledge, with real life and their application in solving problems in various situations.

**Competition 7**

**Communicate and represent, individually and collectively, mathematical concepts, procedures and results using oral, written, graphic and multimedia language, through different types of supports, including technological ones, to give meaning to knowledge, transfer it and share it.**

**Evaluation criteria**

7.1 Show organization when communicating mathematical ideas.

7.2 Use terminology, symbology and mathematical rigor in the communication and representation of mathematics.

7.3 Express mathematical ideas orally with a coherent and precise record.

7.4 Write mathematical texts of all types (descriptive, argumentative, expository, instructive, etc.) with scientific rigor, fluent and coherent reading and in which the use of language and mathematical symbology is precise.

7.5 Design mathematical representations that are capable, on their own, of expressing synthesized mathematical ideas.

7.6 Use artistic and creative expression to communicate, represent and express mathematical ideas and reasoning, such as mathematical photography, mathematical videos, visual works and music.

7.7 Dialogue with peers and debate mathematical ideas to describe, explain and justify reasoning, processes and conclusions.

In the information society, the need for clear and truthful communication, both orally and in writing, is becoming more apparent every day. Interacting with others offers the possibility to exchange ideas and reflect on them, collaborate, cooperate, generate and consolidate new knowledge, making communication an indispensable element in learning mathematics.

Representations of mathematical ideas, concepts and procedures facilitate reasoning and demonstration, are used to examine relationships and test the validity of answers, are naturally present in digital technologies and are at the heart of mathematical communication.

The development of this competence involves expressing facts, ideas, concepts and complex procedures verbally, analytically and graphically, truthfully and precisely, using the appropriate mathematical terminology, giving meaning and permanence to the ideas and making them public.

It also involves increasing the repertoire of mathematical representations and the knowledge of how to use them effectively, emphasizing the ways in which different representations of the same objects can convey different information and showing the importance of selecting representations appropriate to the task.

**Competition 8**

**Develop self-regulation and personal skills that help identify and manage emotions, learning from mistakes and facing situations of uncertainty as an opportunity, to persevere and enjoy the process of learning mathematics.**

**Evaluation criteria**

8.1 Identify the own mistakes made in mathematics, discover the conceptual, procedural or strategic elements that cause them and, finally, express in a reasoned way the reason for the mistake.

8.2 Decide and put into practice specific strategies that allow you to avoid the error and overcome the difficulty.

8.3 Persevere in achieving the objectives by implementing new mathematical strategies by identifying and managing one's emotions.

8.4 Actively participate in the self-evaluation, sharing and agreeing with the teaching staff on improvement strategies.

8.5 Develop the creative capacity by making innovative mathematical proposals related to artistic, cultural, social and technological aspects enjoying the freedom to decide without showing fear of making mistakes.

The resolution of more global problems or challenges in which mathematics is involved often represents a challenge that involves a multitude of emotions that the students must manage correctly. Emotional skills in learning mathematics promote students' well-being, emotional regulation and interest in their learning.

The development of this competence involves identifying and managing emotions in the process of learning mathematics, recognizing sources of stress, being persevering in achieving goals, thinking critically and creatively, creating resilience and maintaining a proactive attitude in the face of new mathematical challenges.

**Competition 9**

**Cooperate, developing the social skills needed to actively participate in inclusive work teams and recognizing the diversity and value of others' contributions, to share and build mathematical knowledge collectively.**

**Evaluation criteria**

9.1 Contribute and share strategies and mathematical reasoning with colleagues, value collective success as a strategy for personal improvement.

9.2 Collaborate in teamwork both in face-to-face and virtual environments, listening to others and valuing their contributions, respecting the gender perspective and multiculturalism, sharing and building mathematical knowledge together.

9.3 Ideate, design and contribute mathematical activities and problems of conceptual quality to the rest of the classmates in order to actively participate in the collective construction of mathematical knowledge.

9.4 Help identify mistakes and learning difficulties of colleagues by making constructive and concrete contributions that can help overcome them and improve.

9.5 Use the Catalan language in learning mathematics as a tool for cohesion, inclusion and equity.

Work on the values ​​of respect, tolerance, equality or peaceful resolution of conflicts, at the same time as solving mathematical challenges by developing effective communication skills, planning, inquiry, motivation and trust, to create healthy relationships and work environments, which allow self-confidence to be strengthened and situations of coexistence in equality to be normalized. Likewise, the breakdown of stereotypes and preconceived ideas about mathematics associated with individual issues, such as gender or aptitude for mathematics, must be encouraged.

The development of this competence involves showing empathy for others, establishing and maintaining positive relationships, exercising active listening and assertive communication, working in a team and making responsible decisions.

**know**

Knowledge, understood as the set of knowledge, skills, values ​​and attitudes, is formulated in relation to contexts in which competence learning can be developed. Teachers can incorporate alternative contexts if they consider it relevant. In order to facilitate learning and the development of the corresponding specific skills, teachers can assess the possibility of organizing the knowledge of the subject, or of the different subjects coordinated in an area, based on situations.

The situations make it possible to program the course of any level, subject or field from a collection or sequence of challenges, contexts and circumstances of the real world, from which derive questions that need to be answered and that intertwine knowledge, that is, knowledge, skills, values and attitudes, with the capacities that support the competence approach to learning, which modifies the usual planning of the acquisition of knowledge and competences based on academic logic specific to the areas of knowledge or subjects, embodied in the traditional sequence of disciplinary subjects. It aims to approach the learner's logic to give meaning to their learning based on the sequence of relevant contexts embodied in the situations.

***Analysis***

**Number Sense**

- Sense of operations
	- Interpretation of numerical information in everyday documents: financial documents, invoices, payroll, news, etc.
	- Use of technological and digital tools to solve numerical problems.
- Relationships/financial education
	- Application of the relationships between ratios, proportions, percentages, rates (both per one, per cent, per thousand, etc.), taxes and absolute and relative increases, in the representation of quantitative relationships in real contexts.
	- Use of proportional reasoning in the resolution of financial problems: means of payment with the collection of interest and commissions, currency exchange, etc., using technological tools.

**Sense of measurement**

- change
	- Study of the absolute variation and the average variation of a function as a preliminary step for the construction of the derivative concept.
	- Construction of the concept of the derivative of a function based on the study of the change of the function in different contexts.

**Algebraic Sense**

- Mathematical model
	- Using dynamic geometry worksheets or spreadsheets to model real-world situations using linear, quadratic, simple rational, exponential, logarithmic, piecewise, and periodic functions.
- Equality and inequality
	- Solving systems of equations and inequalities to solve problems related to modeling or functions in different contexts using digital tools.
- Relations and functions
	- Graphical representation from dynamic geometry tools or tables of values ​​to analyze the properties of function classes, including linear, quadratic, simple rational, exponential, and logarithmic.
	- Interpretation of the properties of a function to solve problems in various contexts.
- Computational thinking
	- Formulation, resolution, analysis, representation and interpretation of relationships and problems in everyday life and in different areas using algorithms, programs and appropriate technological tools.

***Geometry***

**Spatial Sense**

- Visualization, reasoning and geometric modeling
	- Representation of everyday life situations using different types of graphs (directed, planes, weighted, trees, etc.).
	- Solving path and circuit problems using Eulerian and Hamiltonian graphs. Graph coloring.
	- Solving the minimum path problem in different contexts.

***Probability and Statistics***

**Number Sense**

- counting
	- Using basic rules and strategies to compute the cardinality of finite sets to solve problems in diverse contexts.

**Sense of measurement**

- measure
	- Analysis of the uncertainty associated with a random phenomenon by means of probability.

**Sense Stochastic**

- Data organization and analysis
	- Interpretation and analysis of statistical information in various contexts.
	- Organization of data from two-dimensional variables using joint distribution and marginal and conditional distributions. Analysis of statistical dependence.
	- Use and differentiation between linear or quadratic regression for the study of the relationship between two variables, assessing the relevance of the different adjustments.
	- Using the linear correlation coefficient to quantify the linear relationship between two variables. Analysis of their reliability to make predictions in different contexts, in particular scientific and technological ones.
	- Use of the calculator, the spreadsheet or specific software in the analysis of statistical data.
- Predictability and uncertainty
	- Calculation of probabilities in compound experiments through the use of the concept of conditional probability and the independence between random events. Use of tree diagrams and contingency tables as tools to support the calculation of probabilities. Contextualization of the theorem of total probabilities.
- Probability distributions
	- Modeling stochastic phenomena using binomial and normal probability distributions. Calculation of associated probabilities using technological tools.
- inference
	- Design of statistical studies related to various contexts using digital tools. Analysis and assessment of the representativeness of the sample used in a statistical study.

***Social-emotional knowledge***

**Socio-emotional sense**

- Beliefs, attitudes and emotions
	- Self-regulation skills aimed at discovering one's own areas of improvement and personal development.
	- Willingness to delve into certain aspects of mathematical abstraction as the only way to improve its applicability.
	- Perseverance in achieving a goal by exploring and redefining, if necessary, the strategies necessary for personal growth.
	- Creative capacity making innovative mathematical proposals related to artistic, cultural, social and technological aspects in which the enjoyment of doing mathematics is present.
	- Ability to identify own conceptual confusions that determine the mistakes made in mathematics, valuing them as an important source of learning.
- Decision making
	- Ability to put into practice concrete strategies that help to overcome own conceptual confusions.
	- Skills to explore and evaluate different strategies in the mathematical treatment of a problem or situation.
	- Skills in improving learning strategies based on suggestions for improvement made in assessments and co-assessments.
	- Ability to make personal decisions based on the critical analysis of a situation that can be treated with mathematical argumentation.
- Inclusion, respect and diversity
- Ability to listen, respect and try mathematical strategies proposed by another person.
	- Ability to contribute ideas and arguments that help the learning of colleagues.
	- Ability to agree on different opinions and strategies when making a collective decision in the development of a mathematical activity.
	- Appreciation of collective success as an individual success.
	- Appreciation of the contribution of mathematics and the role of mathematicians and mathematics throughout history in multiple aspects that surround us, both in the artistic, cultural, social, scientific and technological fields.

</div>
</div>
</div>

<h2 class="accordion-header" id="headingRob">
<button class="accordion-button collapsed" type="button" data-bs-toggle="collapse" data-bs-target="#collapseRob" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="collapseRob">
<strong>🧬 Biomedicina -  Matèries optatives - Matèries optatives anuals de primer curs</strong>
</button>
</h2>
<div id="collapseRob" class="accordion-collapse collapse" aria-labelledby="headingRob" data-bs-parent="#competenciasAccordion">
<div class="accordion-body">

[**Biomedicina**](https://xtec.gencat.cat/web/.content/curriculum/batxillerat/curriculum-171-2022/materias-optatives/materias-optatives-anuals-de-1r-curs/Biomedicina.pdf){target="_blank"}

The subject of Biomedicine is an annual optional subject that is particularly recommended for students with an orientation towards biosanitary studies. However, it can be taken by any student from other modes of high school.

It starts from the competences achieved by students in the subject of Biology and Geology throughout Compulsory Secondary Education and deepens some topics in this field of knowledge, especially those related to health and disease, to achieve the competence learning specific to the high school stage.

Biomedicine is a discipline that studies the biological aspects of medicine, essentially through the analysis of the genetic, cellular, biochemical and molecular factors of the human body and also of the diseases that can potentially affect it.

In the development of the subject, the study of processes specific to the state of health is combined with situations that alter its normal functioning.

The purpose of the subject is not to cover the global study of the specific functions of the human body, nor of the set of diseases that can affect it, nor of the range of therapies that are applied to it.

The different knowledge blocks of the subject pursue the achievement of specific skills, based on the presentation and work with a collection of cases throughout the course, so that the students can identify and relate the different elements and processes involved in each of the situations.

Thus, the cellular, physiological or genetic aspects, the alterations resulting from some affectation and the applied therapies are studied in context, based on a case or a real or plausible situation.

The organization of the classroom in autonomous work groups that approach the study of specific cases to share the essential elements of each one is particularly suitable for the development of the subject.

The specific competences of the subject connect with those of the subject of Biology, affecting the integrated application of the learning achieved in problems specific to the vital functions of the human organism, in the understanding of the biological processes that support the state of health and its alterations, in the knowledge of the applications of the different modern therapies and in the assessment of their benefits, risks and ethical implications, if this is the case.

The blocks that organize the knowledge of the subject have been structured around a selection of contents that should be articulated in the cases that the professors put to the students.

Thus, the first block focuses on the study of blood, its elements, its functions and also its renewal process. It includes the analysis of the main diseases that can affect this tissue and the specific study of some of them, analyzing causes, alterations and applicable therapies.

The second block focuses on the study of the nervous system based on the ability to react to external stimuli. The relationship of the nervous system with the effector organs and, specifically, with any alteration related to muscle atrophy, its causes and consequences and the effect that possible gene and cell therapies would have.

The third block affects the immune system of people. The objects of study will be the processes related to the body's reaction to the presence of an infectious agent, the mechanism of action of the different types of vaccines and some example of an autoimmune disease.

The fourth block studies the differences in the sexual development of people, the different situations, the diversity of causes that can originate them and the key genetic factors involved. That is why it will be essential to distinguish between chromosomal sex, gonadal sex, sexual identity and sexual orientation of people.

The fifth block deals with cancer, in its relationship with the alteration of some genes, in the causes that originate it and in its distinction from benign tumors. At the end of the case being studied, it will be necessary to introduce the diagnostic methods and the different treatments: surgery, chemotherapy, radiotherapy and biological therapy (hormone therapy, immunotherapy).

The teaching staff will establish the evaluation criteria for each of the specific skills and will select the knowledge and methodological approaches they consider most appropriate based on the guidelines present in this same document.

**Specific skills**

**Competition 1**

Apply autonomously and in an integrated manner the learning developed and the various forms of reasoning and research typical of biology to carry out experimental research and observational studies on problems related to the vital functions of the human being and others that relate health to lifestyles and consumption habits.

**Competition 2**

Analyze situations that occur throughout people's lives, both in their state of health and in situations of illness, in order to understand and relate the biological processes in which changes in health states are sustained, as well as the normal development, growth, aging and inheritance of characters in humans.

**Competition 3**

Explain the biological foundations of some recent contributions of biomedical research, such as gene and cell therapies, new vaccines and new medicines, and evaluate and provide arguments about the possible benefits, risks, consequences and ethical implications of their application in order to take a position in the social debate regarding the social and ethical implications of these therapies.

<h2 class="accordion-header" id="headingRob">
<button class="accordion-button collapsed" type="button" data-bs-toggle="collapse" data-bs-target="#collapseRob" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="collapseRob">
<strong>🖥️ Programació -  Matèries optatives - Matèries optatives anuals de primer curs</strong>
</button>
</h2>
<div id="collapseRob" class="accordion-collapse collapse" aria-labelledby="headingRob" data-bs-parent="#competenciasAccordion">
<div class="accordion-body">

[**Programació**](https://xtec.gencat.cat/web/.content/curriculum/batxillerat/curriculum-171-2022/materias-optatives/materias-optatives-anuals-de-1r-curs/Programacio.docx.pdf){target="_blank"}

Programming is an annual optional subject that can be taken by students from any type of high school. The ability to program provides added value to students in the higher studies that they can take later.

It starts from the digital skills acquired related to computational thinking and programming throughout compulsory secondary education and presents a global view of current programming languages ​​and their fields of application.

There is a growing demand for competent personnel in the development of personalized applications aimed at new situations and in the introduction of improvements in the design, functionality and usability of existing ones. This demand affects all areas of knowledge and research, both in the scientific and technological side (basic and applied science, medicine, engineering, etc.) and in the humanistic and social side (economics, relational, artistic creation, etc.). Indeed, programming contributes to the creation of programs, applications and web services that make daily life more comfortable, facilitate our personal relationships and allow us to access a wide variety of services (databases, telemedicine, banking, etc.).

In this subject, students are asked to develop a program, an application or a web service throughout the course using a specific programming language and environment. Nevertheless, the subject exposes the different areas where applications need to be programmed and the most appropriate and common programming languages ​​in each case.

The decision on the characteristics and functionalities of an application to be developed must be based on the specific situation to be solved and the target audience to which it is addressed. It is therefore necessary to learn and know how to apply situation analysis techniques and subsequently identify the programming environment that must allow the development of the required solution.

The rapid evolution of programming platforms means that new ones often appear and others become obsolete. This reality must be kept in mind and students must be presented with the basic principles of prototyping in the design of interfaces and generic programming strategies, present on any platform.

During compulsory secondary education, students will preferably have programmed in environments based on block programming, such as Scratch and/or App Inventor. In high school, therefore, it is convenient to start programming using code.

Today's variety of operating systems makes developing the same program for each in native form too ambitious a goal for a school project. In this sense, platforms that allow the creation of executables for several systems from a single source code should be favored. The task of developing a program or mobile application is usually complex and requires modularity and teamwork to ensure the achievement of the goal.

The knowledge of the subject is organized in four blocks:

The first block, *computational thinking and programming*, aims to understand the fundamentals of algorithms for the design and development of programs, and the application of specific techniques such as the elaboration of flow diagrams and the encapsulation of properties, functions and events in the definition of programming objects.

In the second block, *programming languages ​​and environments*, the programming languages ​​most used today are listed, classifying them according to typology and scope of application. The main characteristics of each and the corresponding programming environments are detailed.

In the third block, *prototyping and design of user interfaces*, the procedures to follow to obtain a suitable user interface for each program or application are indicated. It focuses on navigation, on-screen layout of components and styles.

In the fourth block, *development of local applications and in the cloud*, the particularities to be taken into account in the development of programs that must be run on specific client devices and in which they offer services in the cloud, such as access to databases or web applications, are described.

The teaching staff will establish the evaluation criteria for each of the specific skills and will select the knowledge and methodological approaches they consider most appropriate based on the guidelines presented in this same document.

**Specific skills**

**Competition 1**

Analyze real situations that may require an IT solution. Detect the functional needs of situations and, taking into account the characteristics of potential users, propose solutions in the form of programs, applications or web services.

**Competition 2**

Create visual prototypes of programs and applications and use them to create user interfaces with the appropriate IT tools.

**Competition 3**

Starting from the functional description of an IT solution, develop the program, application or web service that implements them using an appropriate programming language and environment.

<h2 class="accordion-header" id="headingRob">
<button class="accordion-button collapsed" type="button" data-bs-toggle="collapse" data-bs-target="#collapseRob" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="collapseRob">
<strong>🖥️ Matemàtica Aplicada -  Matèries optatives trimestrals de primer curs</strong>
</button>
</h2>
<div id="collapseRob" class="accordion-collapse collapse" aria-labelledby="headingRob" data-bs-parent="#competenciasAccordion">
<div class="accordion-body">

[**Applied Mathematics**](https://xtec.gencat.cat/web/.content/curriculum/batxillerat/curriculum-171-2022/materias-optatives/materias-optatives-trimestrals-de-primer-curs/Matematica-Aplicada_TS_sc.docx.pdf){target="_blank"}

The Applied Mathematics subject is a quarterly optional subject focused on providing a panoramic view of the field of application of mathematics that allows students to ascertain and arouse interest in mathematics, in particular its use in many other disciplines as an instrumental subject that works with numbers, magnitudes or quantifiable elements.

Quarterly optional subjects, such as Applied Mathematics, are structured from three thematic blocks, also of quarterly duration, which each educational center will configure in accordance with its curriculum project.

Today, mathematics is applied in various fields and acquires value, since the great global challenges, such as respect for the environment, energy efficiency or inclusive and sustainable industrialization, which society will have to face, require people with the ability to adapt to changing conditions, to learn autonomously, to model situations, to explore new avenues of research and to use technology effectively. In this sense, the use of mathematical knowledge and skills, such as reasoning, modelling, computational thinking or problem solving, is very appropriate.

In this optional quarterly subject, the mathematical knowledge that is included are the tools that allow you to solve with scientific rigor the challenges or questions that arise from situations outside of mathematics.

Examples of some questions or challenges that require the application of mathematics to solve them and can be a starting learning situation for the different thematic axes of each term:

- How does artificial intelligence recognize in which language a text is written? What criteria are used to classify and sort the books and magazines in a library? How are they coded in a database to have them located? (Library and documentation).
- Why do credit cards have a verification number that only the owner knows? How many digits does it have to be secure enough? What is the probability that by putting a number at random we guess the code? How are secret codes created and read? (Cryptography).
- Archeological digs on a grid? How to reconstruct the shape of a vase from an archaeological remains? What math do archaeologists use? (Mathematics for archaeology).
- How can large data sets be explored and analyzed to model trends? What programming languages ​​can be useful for analyzing and making databases more visual? (Big data).
- What basic meteorological data make it possible to understand the variability and climate change observed in Catalonia from the historical climate series recovered and analyzed by the Meteorological Service of Catalonia? (Climate change).
- What bases does an insurance company apply to establish the quotas of its insurances? Why are insurance companies reluctant to sell motorcycle insurance to young people? (Insurance).
- What statistical data are key in the evolution of a pandemic? What statistical tools are used to analyze the data and make decisions? (The data: keys in pandemics).
- What mathematical approaches try to model the flow of vehicular traffic based on some of its characteristics? Macroscopic models, microscopic models and mesoscopic or kinetic models (Traffic control processes).
- What data must be collected to study the evolution of a crop and know the amount of irrigation it needs? How can you monitor the amount of fertilizer a field needs? Is it possible to control the degree of wine that will come out of a vineyard by collecting certain data on the evolution of the crop? (Mathematics in the evolution of crops).

Educational centers can choose any of the challenges presented to articulate the sequence of thematic blocks that will integrate the subject. They can also formulate other different subject challenges that they consider relevant.

The challenges that each center selects will be organized in such a way that students must:

- Handle information from various sources by identifying, analyzing, selecting, contrasting, combining and communicating information in different formats to generate knowledge in the context of responding to a problem, in a broad sense.
- Mobilize the acquired knowledge and learning of a cognitive or instrumental nature specific to the field of knowledge, as well as handle the available resources and different forms of reasoning, to interpret and respond to a variety of situations (problems, research, cases, controversies...).
- Review, structure and evaluate with ethical and logical criteria ideas, thoughts or reasoning, own or others, in diverse contexts, local or global, of a varied nature, making justified and coherent proposals for action.

The teaching staff must establish the evaluation criteria for each of the specific skills that will be adapted to each challenge and must select the knowledge and methodological approaches that they consider most appropriate based on the guidelines of this same document.

**Specific skills**

**Competition 1**

Identify, select, organize and critically evaluate information, checking its reliability, to solve questions raised independently and create content related to the application of mathematics.

 **Competition 2**

Apply the learning in an integrated way and the various forms of mathematical reasoning, to pose and solve problems of various disciplines and fields that use mathematical tools by searching for and using the appropriate strategies, critically analyzing the solutions and reformulating the procedure, if necessary.

**Competition 3**

Identify and use the ideas, evidence and arguments that use any of the different mathematical senses (numerical, algebraic, spatial, metric, stochastic and socio-affective), which support the explanation of phenomena and processes from different disciplines to adopt a personal position and interpretation based on scientific and mathematical criteria.

<h2 class="accordion-header" id="headingRob">

<div id="collapseRob" class="accordion-collapse collapse" aria-labelledby="headingRob" data-bs-parent="#competenciasAccordion">

[**Current Scientific Challenges (Biology and Geology)**](https://xtec.gencat.cat/web/.content/curriculum/batxillerat/curriculum-171-2022/materias-optatives/materias-optatives-trimestrals-de-primer-curs/Reptes-Cientificas-Actuals-Biologia-i-Geologia_TS_sc.pdf){target="_blank"}

The subject Challenges in Biology and Geology is a quarterly optional subject focused on providing a panoramic view of the field of study of these sciences that allows students to ascertain, awaken, or discard in their case, interest in these disciplines.

The quarterly optional subjects, such as Challenges in Biology and Geology, are structured from three thematic blocks, also of quarterly duration, which each educational center will configure in accordance with its curriculum project.

Biology is the science that studies life, including the processes, systems, functions, mechanisms or other biological characters underlying living things in various specialized fields including, for example, morphology, physiology, development or evolution. A multitude of disciplines are derived from biology, among which stand out biochemistry, the biology of organisms and populations, human biology, medical sciences and environmental sciences. The development these sciences have acquired is a consequence of the multitude of challenges they have had to address and are still facing, such as:

- How do genetic and environmental components interact throughout the organism's development to form an individual? Are we predetermined by our genes? (From the zygote to the individual).
- What are the latest therapeutic advances that make it possible to cure certain types of cancer or prevent hereditary genetic diseases? (Therapeutic advances).
- How is balance maintained in natural systems and what role do the interactions between the different populations that are part of it play? Can this balance be restored if it is disturbed? (Equilibrium in natural systems).
- What are our origins? When, where and, above all, from which species of pre-human hominid did the human race emerge? Who were the first human beings? How did our species originate? And more importantly: what is a "human being"? (The origin of humans).

Geology, understood in a broad sense, is made up of a set of disciplines whose object is the study of planet Earth, of its interactions with the living beings that inhabit it and with the rest of the Universe. Thus, we can understand that it encompasses a series of disciplines such as, among others, geosciences, atmospheric and marine sciences, environmental sciences and planetary sciences.

Each of these disciplines poses several challenges such as those detailed in the following list:

- Can natural disasters be predicted? Can the effects on the population of earthquakes, tsunamis, volcanic eruptions, torrential rains and floods be reduced? (Natural disasters).
- How can we mitigate the effects of global climate change by increasing green alternatives in cities or generating electricity from solar and wind energy? (Deconstructing climate change).
- How does the interior of the Earth work? How can this be investigated and how does it affect the earth's surface? (What is and what happens inside the Earth).
- What is the geology of other planets, solar and extrasolar? How can we come to obtain evidence and what importance can they have in relation to the possible existence of life outside the Earth? (Planetary Geology).

Educational centers can choose any of the challenges presented to articulate the sequence of thematic blocks that will integrate the subject. They can also formulate other different subject challenges that they consider relevant.

The challenges that each center selects will be organized in such a way that students must:

- Handle information from various sources by identifying, analyzing, selecting, contrasting, combining and communicating information in different formats to generate knowledge in the context of responding to a problem, in a broad sense.
- Mobilize the acquired knowledge and learning of a cognitive or instrumental nature specific to the field of knowledge, as well as handle the available resources and different forms of reasoning, to interpret and respond to a variety of situations (problems, research, cases, controversies...).
- Review, structure and evaluate with ethical and logical criteria ideas, thoughts or reasoning, own or others, in diverse contexts, local or global, of a varied nature, making justified and coherent proposals for action.

The teaching staff must establish the evaluation criteria for each of the specific skills that will be adapted to each challenge and must select the knowledge and methodological approaches that they consider most appropriate based on the guidelines of this same document.

**Specific skills**

**Competition 1**

Identify, select, organize and critically evaluate information, contrasting its reliability to solve questions raised independently and create content related to biology and geology.

**Competition 2**

Apply the learning in an integrated way and the various forms of reasoning typical of science, to raise and solve problems related to biology and geology, searching for and using the appropriate strategies, critically analyzing the solutions and reformulating the procedure, if necessary.

**Competition 3**

Identify and use the ideas, evidence, scientific arguments that support the explanation of phenomena and processes related to biology and geology to adopt a personal position and interpretation based on scientific criteria.

[**Current Scientific Challenges (Physics and Chemistry)**](https://xtec.gencat.cat/web/.content/curriculum/batxillerat/curriculum-171-2022/materias-optatives/materias-optatives-trimestrals-de-primer-curs/Reptes-Cientific-Actuals-Fisica-i-Quimica_TS_sc.pdf){target="_blank"}

The subject Challenges in Physics and Chemistry is a quarterly optional subject focused on providing a panoramic view of the field of study of these sciences that allows students to ascertain, awaken, or discard in their case, interest in these disciplines.

Quarterly optional subjects, such as Challenges in Physics and Chemistry, are structured around three thematic blocks, also of quarterly duration, which each educational center will set up in accordance with its curriculum project.

Physics is a science that provides applications for the improvement of life and the environment, as well as the theoretical foundation for research on the Universe. Its applications in the field of energy, electromagnetism, forces and movement cover a wide range of practical solutions to everyday problems, such as the mechanical generation of electricity with the most efficient and sustainable processes, the optimization and utilization of heat transfers, the foundation of a multitude of medical techniques for diagnosis and treatment, the synthesis of new elements in synchrotrons, and nuclear fusion. On the other hand, astrophysics, the physics of high energies and elementary particles contribute to discoveries about the cosmos and the forces of the Universe. The development of the physical sciences contributes to scientific-technological progress that allows addressing a multitude of present and future challenges.

In each of these areas of action, several challenges arise, such as those detailed below:

- Which electricity generation processes have the least impact on the environment and why? Which processes are more efficient? How can heat transfers be used? How can renewable energies, such as wind and solar, contribute to the energy transition? (Efficiency and energy transition).
- Why does aeronautics and the science of satellites and spacecraft become key in today's society? What is the European Space Agency? What tasks and investigations are carried out there? What can the data collected there be useful for humanity? What are they and what can be done with space debris? Will they always be in orbit? (Aeronautics and space research).
- What does astrophysics study and what does it give us? What nuclear reactions occur in stars? What changes occur in the Universe and in the bodies that make it up? What does this knowledge contribute to scientific knowledge and what applications do they revert to in society? (Astrophysics and cosmology).
- What are the aims and purposes of high energy physics and what does it contribute to society? What are and what is the purpose of particle accelerators and specifically the European Organization for Nuclear Research (CERN)? What evidence do they give us? What is and what has been the purpose of synchrotrons? What is done at the Alba synchrotron? (High energy physics and particle accelerators).
- How does quantum physics contribute to the development of new microscopic techniques? What are the differences and similarities between the foundations and the images they provide? How does quantum mechanics contribute to the development of new microscopic techniques?
- What can quantum computing bring? Can cold fusion provide a solution to today's energy problems? (Quantum physics at the service of humanity).

Chemistry is a scientific discipline that contributes, among others, to the progress and well-being of people and to the prevention and reversal of environmental problems. This is why the development of skills in the field of the transformation of matter, knowledge of its properties, structure and interactions is key. Chemistry provides knowledge applied to the circular economy, the design and synthesis of new materials, the preservation of the quality of air and natural and drinking water and their treatments, renewable energies and energy vectors, new biofuels and biomaterials, as well as contributions from nanoscience and nanotechnology applied both in the field of the environment and biomedicine. The development of the chemical sciences contributes to the scientific and technological progress that makes it possible to address a multitude of present and future challenges.

In each of these areas of action, several challenges arise, such as those detailed below:

- What are the consequences of not reusing and/or not recycling? Why are responsible consumption habits necessary? How do transformation processes from raw materials impact energy and water consumption, environmental pollution and quality of life? How can we profit and at the same time avoid the impact of waste biomaterials to generate biofuels, bioplastics, etc.? (Circular economy and responsible consumption).
- What are the causes of the average global increase in planetary temperature and what actions can we take to stop this increase? Which decarbonisation strategies are the most appropriate, and how and why do they directly contribute to reversing the climate emergency? What environmental impact can batteries have and how can sustainable use be optimized? How can renewable energies and energy-saving habits contribute to alleviate the problem? (Sustainable energies to mitigate the climate emergency).
- What are the causes of the differences in air and water quality in different places? What human activities affect air and water quality to varying degrees? What parameters determine these alterations and how can they be evaluated over time? How can these problems be minimized? (Air quality and means of transport. Sanitation and water quality).
- How do new advances in the synthesis of nanoparticles and nanomaterials and in nanoscale sensors contribute to personal and global health and to generating drugs with fewer side effects? What advances in chemistry applied to the nano world have a direct impact on environmental issues? (The world of chemical nanostructures at the service of people and the environment).

Educational centers can choose any of the challenges presented to articulate the sequence of thematic blocks that will integrate the subject. They can also formulate other different subject challenges that they consider relevant.

The challenges that each center selects will be organized in such a way that students must:

- Handle information from various sources by identifying, analyzing, selecting, contrasting, combining and communicating information in different formats to generate knowledge in the context of responding to a problem, in a broad sense.
- Mobilize the acquired knowledge and learning of a cognitive or instrumental nature specific to the field of knowledge, as well as handle the available resources and different forms of reasoning, to interpret and respond to a variety of situations (problems, research, cases, controversies...).
- Review, structure and evaluate with ethical and logical criteria ideas, thoughts or reasoning, own or others, in diverse contexts, local or global, of a varied nature, making justified and coherent proposals for action.

The teaching staff must establish the evaluation criteria for each of the specific skills that will be adapted to each challenge and must select the knowledge and methodological approaches that they consider most appropriate based on the guidelines of this same document.

**Specific skills**

**Competition 1**

Identify, select, organize and critically evaluate information, contrasting its reliability to solve questions raised independently and create content related to physics and chemistry.

**Competition 2**

Apply learning in an integrated way and the various forms of reasoning typical of science, to pose and solve problems related to physics and chemistry, searching for and using the appropriate strategies, critically analyzing the solutions and reformulating the procedure, if necessary.

**Competition 3**

Identify and use the ideas, evidence, scientific arguments that support the explanation of phenomena and processes related to physics and chemistry to adopt a personal position and interpretation based on scientific criteria.
